A locator specifically supporting random reshuffling is required.

children.title: Without-Replacement Mini-Batches
children.top_down_role: Partial finite-population batches sampled without repeated indices.

knowledge_statements.title: Without-Replacement Mini-Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjoint mini-batches drawn from a finite population within each epoch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), and let \(b\) divide \(n\). At epoch \(s\), sample a permutation \(\pi_s\) and form disjoint batches \(B_{s,k}=\{\pi_s((k-1)b+1),\ldots,\pi_s(kb)\}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,n/b\). Starting from \(x_{s,0}\), compute \(G_{s,k}=b^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_{s,k}}\nabla f_i(x_{s,k-1})\) and update \(x_{s,k}=x_{s,k-1}-\eta_{s,k}G_{s,k}\). Continue through the epoch and output the final or prescribed averaged iterate after a fixed number of epochs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition a random permutation into disjoint mini-batches, average each batch’s component gradients, and process every component once per epoch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{s,1},\ldots,B_{s,n/b}\) are disjoint and their union is \(\{1,ldots,n\}\).
review_flags: exact without-replacement mini-batch source locator missing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The without-replacement mini-batch algorithm lacks a citation. Its conclusion also contains \(ldots\) rather than \(\ldots\), so the displayed union is malformed.

children.title: Epoch-Level Dependence
children.top_down_role: Within-epoch dependence induced by finite-population sampling.

knowledge_statements.title: Epoch-Level Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional dependence induced by sampling without replacement inside an epoch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_{s,1},\ldots,I_{s,n}\) be a uniformly random permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(\mathcal{F}_{s,k}=\sigma(I_{s,1},\ldots,I_{s,k})\). For \(k<n\), conditional on \(\mathcal{F}_{s,k}\), the next index is uniform only over the unused set \(R_{s,k}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{I_{s,1},\ldots,I_{s,k}\}\): \(\mathbb{P}(I_{s,k+1}=i\mid\mathcal{F}_{s,k})=|R_{s,k}|^{-1}\) for \(i\in R_{s,k}\), and zero otherwise. Consequently, within-epoch component choices are dependent, even when independently sampled permutations make different epochs independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After some components have been processed, the next index is uniform only among unused components; hence draws within an epoch are dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{s,k+1}\) is generally not independent of \(\mathcal{F}_{s,k}\).

notation.meaning: history of indices revealed in epoch s through position k
set of indices unused at position k
index occupying position k of epoch s

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional distribution and within-epoch dependence property are correct for a uniform random permutation, but no source or standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Permutation-Sensitive Behavior
children.top_down_role: Performance variation attributable to ordering within sampled epochs.

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation-Sensitive Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-component quadratic example whose epoch endpoint depends on processing order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb{R}\), let \(f_1(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2\), \(f_2(x)=\tfrac12(x+1)^2\), and use constant step size \(\eta\in(0,1)\). Starting from the same \(x_0\), one epoch of component-gradient updates in order \((1,2)\) gives \(x_2^{(1,2)}=(1-\eta)^2x_0-\eta^2\), whereas order \((2,1)\) gives \(x_2^{(2,1)}=(1-\eta)^2x_0+\eta^2\). Thus \(x_2^{(2,1)}-x_2^{(1,2)}=2\eta^2\neq 0\), although each order uses both components exactly once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two shifted quadratics, reversing the component order changes the one-epoch endpoint by twice the squared step size.

notation.meaning: epoch endpoint under component order 1 then 2
epoch endpoint under component order 2 then 1

review_flags: counterexample is directly checkable but external source locator missing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic counterexample and its endpoint calculations are internally correct, and counterexample is the proper content kind, but the record supplies neither an external source nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Importance-Weighted Sampling Family
children.top_down_role: Sampling distributions adapted to component smoothness, scale, or variance.

children.title: Importance-Weighted Sampling
children.top_down_role: Component sampling paired with probability-based estimator correction.

knowledge_statements.title: Importance-Weighted Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased finite-sum gradient estimation under nonuniform component sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), choose probabilities \(p_i>0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\). At iteration \(t\), draw \(I_t\) independently with \(\mathbb{P}(I_t=i)=p_i\), form \(G_t=(np_{I_t})^{-1}\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)\), and update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tG_t\). Then \(\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid x_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\). Initialize at a specified \(x_0\), repeat for \(T\) iterations, and output \(x_T\) or a prescribed weighted average of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample components nonuniformly and divide each sampled gradient by its sampling weight, producing an unbiased finite-sum gradient estimator.
assumptions_latex: \(I_t\) is conditionally independent of the past given \(x_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[(np_{I_t})^{-1}\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)\mid x_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The importance-weighted estimator and unbiasedness identity are correct under the stated positive probabilities and conditional sampling assumptions, but the algorithm has no citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Smoothness-Proportional Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling distributions shaped by component regularity scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness-Proportional Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling probabilities that equalize component smoothness divided by probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each differentiable component \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) have an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient, with \(L_i>0\). Among probability vectors \(p\) satisfying \(p_i>0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\), the probabilities \(p_i=L_i/\sum_{j=1}^nL_j\) minimize \(\max_i L_i/(np_i)\). At this choice every ratio equals \(n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nL_j\), and for every admissible \(p\), \(\max_i L_i/(np_i)\geq n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nL_j\). These probabilities may therefore be used in the importance-weighted estimator \((np_I)^{-1}\nabla f_I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling component i proportionally to its gradient-Lipschitz constant minimizes the largest smoothness-to-probability ratio and equalizes that ratio across components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_i=L_i/\sum_jL_j\) minimizes \(\max_i L_i/(np_i)\), with minimum \(n^{-1}\sum_jL_j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimax calculation is mathematically correct, but it is an optimization result rather than merely a property and requires a supporting source. A theorem or principle kind would better match the asserted minimization statement.

children.title: Variance-Aware Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling distributions shaped by component noise magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Aware Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-moment-optimal probabilities for an importance-weighted finite-sum estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and let \(v_i(x)=\mathbb{E}[\|Z_i(x)\|_2^2]\in(0,+\infty)\), where \(Z_i(x)\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\nabla f_i(x)\). If \(I\) has probabilities \(p_i>0\), then \(G=(np_I)^{-1}Z_I(x)\) has second moment \(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_2^2=n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(x)/p_i\). Over the probability simplex, this quantity is minimized by \(p_i=\sqrt{v_i(x)}/\sum_{j=1}^n\sqrt{v_j(x)}\), and its minimum equals \(n^{-2}(\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{v_i(x)})^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Importance sampling proportional to each component estimator’s root second moment minimizes the aggregate estimator’s second moment at a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_i\propto\sqrt{v_i(x)}\) minimizes \(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_2^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The second-moment formula and minimizing probabilities are correct for the stated fixed-point model, but the minimization result lacks a source and is more naturally a theorem or principle than a generic property.

children.title: Weight-Degeneracy Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instability regimes caused by highly uneven probabilities or correction weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Degeneracy Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unbiasedness or finite variance when importance probabilities vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), the importance-weighted estimator \(G=(np_I)^{-1}
abla f_I(x)\) requires \(p_i>0\) for every component with \(
abla f_i(x)
eq 0\). If such a component has \(p_i=0\), its contribution is never sampled and the stated estimator is undefined there or omits that contribution, so unbiasedness generally fails. If \(p_j\downarrow0\) while \(\|
abla f_j(x)\|_2>0\), then \(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_2^2=n^{-2}\sum_i\|
abla f_i(x)\|_2^2/p_i	o+infty\). Thus a positive lower probability bound prevents this weight-degeneracy mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero probability can destroy unbiasedness, while probabilities approaching zero make the importance-weighted estimator’s second moment diverge whenever the corresponding gradient remains nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_j\downarrow0\) implies \(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_2^2\to+infty\), and \(p_j=0\) generally invalidates unbiased importance weighting.

notation.meaning: probability assigned to the degenerating component

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the appropriate kind, but no source supports the claim. The final statement about a positive lower probability bound should also be understood together with finite component-gradient norms; the bound alone does not generally guarantee a finite second moment.

children.title: State-Adaptive Sampling Family
children.top_down_role: Sampling policies evolving with optimization state or estimator history.

children.title: History-Adaptive Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling distributions updated from past estimator behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: History-Adaptive Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predictable sampling kernels depending on the complete observed history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0}\) be a filtration and let \(I_{k+1}\) take values in a measurable index space \((\mathsf I,\mathcal I)\). Sampling is history-adaptive if there exists an \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable probability kernel \(Q_k(\omega,\cdot)\) such that, for every \(A\in\mathcal I\), \[\mathbb P(I_{k+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_k)=Q_k(A)\quad\text{almost surely}.\] Thus the distribution chosen at time \(k\) may depend on all information revealed through time \(k\), but not on unrevealed future randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, the next sample distribution may depend measurably on the entire observed past, while remaining independent of unrevealed information conditionally on that past.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_k\) is an \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable probability kernel on \((\mathsf I,\mathcal I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(I_{k+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_k)=Q_k(A)\) almost surely for every \(A\in\mathcal I\).

notation.meaning: Next sampled index or observation label

children.title: Iterate-Dependent Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling distributions determined by the current optimization state.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate-Dependent Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-adaptive sampling whose kernel depends on the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_k\) be an \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable iterate in a measurable state space \((\mathsf X,\mathcal X)\). Sampling is iterate-dependent if a Markov kernel \(Q_k:\mathsf X\times\mathcal I\to[0,1]\) satisfies \[\mathbb P(I_{k+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_k)=Q_k(X_k,A)\quad\text{almost surely}\] for every \(A\in\mathcal I\). Conditional on \(X_k\), no other feature of the recorded history changes the prescribed distribution of \(I_{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The next sample is drawn from a probability kernel evaluated at the current iterate; past information affects sampling only through that iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_k\) is a Markov kernel from \((\mathsf X,\mathcal X)\) to \((\mathsf I,\mathcal I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(I_{k+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_k)=Q_k(X_k,A)\) almost surely for all \(A\in\mathcal I\).

children.title: Feedback-Driven Sampling
children.top_down_role: Selection policies responding to observed loss or gradient signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Feedback-Driven Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling probabilities updated from observed oracle feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(X_0\), scores \(S_0\), a filtration \((\mathcal F_k)\), kernels \(Q_k(\cdot\mid X_k,S_k)\), and update maps \(U_k\), repeat: draw \(I_{k+1}\) conditionally according to \(Q_k(\cdot\mid X_k,S_k)\); observe oracle feedback \(Y_{k+1}\); update \(X_{k+1}\) by the chosen stochastic-approximation rule; and set \[S_{k+1}=U_k(S_k,X_k,I_{k+1},Y_{k+1}).\] Require \((X_k,S_k)\) to be \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable. Stop by a prescribed budget or stopping time and output the final or averaged iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method samples using scores computed from previous oracle outcomes, then updates both the optimization iterate and those scores after receiving new feedback.
assumptions_latex: The stopping rule is fixed in advance or is a stopping time for \((\mathcal F_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{k+1}\sim Q_k(\cdot\mid X_k,S_k)\) conditionally on \(\mathcal F_k\), and \(S_{k+1}=U_k(S_k,X_k,I_{k+1},Y_{k+1})\).

notation.meaning: Feedback-derived sampling state or score vector

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind reasonably represents a feedback-driven sampling procedure, but no authoritative source or inspectable locator supports this particular generic algorithmic family.

children.title: Adaptive Selection Bias
children.top_down_role: Estimator distortion introduced by state-responsive sample selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Selection Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias created when adaptive selection changes the conditional oracle mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let component observations satisfy \(\mathbb E[G(x,I)]=g(x)\) under a reference distribution \(p\). If an adaptive rule instead uses \(Q_k(\cdot)=\mathbb P(I_{k+1}\in\cdot\mid\mathcal F_k)\), then the unweighted estimator has conditional bias \[b_k=\mathbb E[G(X_k,I_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]-g(X_k)=\int G(X_k,i)\,Q_k(di)-g(X_k).\] Unless \(b_k=0\) almost surely, or valid importance weights restore the reference expectation, the usual martingale-difference noise condition fails and convergence results requiring conditional unbiasedness do not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive selection is biased when its conditional sample distribution changes the oracle mean; without correction, standard unbiased-noise convergence guarantees become unavailable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(b_k\ne0\) with positive probability, then \(G(X_k,I_{k+1})-g(X_k)\) is not a martingale difference relative to \((\mathcal F_k)\).

children.title: Robbins–Monro Approximation
children.top_down_role: Direct noisy-observation root-finding and its optimization specializations.

knowledge_statements.title: Robbins–Monro Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical stochastic root finding with direct noisy mean-field observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) and seek \(x^\star\) satisfying \(h(x^\star)=0\). Given \(X_0\), positive gains \((a_k)\), and observations \(Y_{k+1}=h(X_k)+M_{k+1}\), perform \[X_{k+1}=X_k-a_kY_{k+1}.\] Here \(X_k\) is \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable and \(\mathbb E[M_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\). A constrained version replaces the update by projection onto the feasible set. Stop at a prescribed iteration or stopping time and output \(X_K\), or a declared average of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robbins–Monro repeatedly subtracts a decreasing gain times a noisy observation of the mean field whose root is sought.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_{k+1}=X_k-a_kY_{k+1}\) is the Robbins–Monro recursion for solving \(h(x)=0\).

notation.meaning: Mean field whose zero is sought

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly describes a standard Robbins–Monro recursion, but no source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Kiefer–Wolfowitz Approximation
children.top_down_role: Finite-difference approximation without direct gradient observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Kiefer–Wolfowitz Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate finite-difference stochastic approximation from noisy function values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To minimize \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), choose \(X_0\), gains \(a_k>0\), radii \(c_k>0\), and noisy values \(Z(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon(x)\). For each coordinate \(j\), form \[\widehat g_{k,j}=\frac{Z(X_k+c_ke_j)-Z(X_k-c_ke_j)}{2c_k},\] and update \[X_{k+1}=X_k-a_k\widehat g_k.\] A constrained variant projects this point onto the feasible set. After a prescribed budget, output the final or specified averaged iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kiefer–Wolfowitz estimates every gradient coordinate by two noisy symmetric function evaluations and takes a stochastic descent step.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is defined on neighborhoods containing \(X_k\pm c_ke_j\).
The noisy function evaluations are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimator uses \(2d\) function evaluations per iteration and the recursion is \(X_{k+1}=X_k-a_k\widehat g_k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise finite-difference algorithm fits the container, but it lacks a source and does not specify the noise coupling convention underlying the two evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous-Perturbation Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-evaluation gradient approximation using a random simultaneous perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To minimize \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), choose \(X_0\), \(a_k,c_k>0\), and perturbations \(\Delta_k\) with nonzero coordinates. Obtain noisy values \(Z_k^+=Z(X_k+c_k\Delta_k)\) and \(Z_k^-=Z(X_k-c_k\Delta_k)\), define \[\widehat g_{k,j}=\frac{Z_k^+-Z_k^-}{2c_k\Delta_{k,j}},\qquad j=1,\ldots,d,\] and set \(X_{k+1}=X_k-a_k\widehat g_k\). Stop after a prescribed budget and output the final or specified averaged iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous perturbation estimates all gradient coordinates from two noisy function values, regardless of dimension, then performs a stochastic descent update.
assumptions_latex: The two noisy function evaluations are integrable.
\(X_k\pm c_k\Delta_k\) lie in the oracle domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration constructs \(\widehat g_k\) from two function evaluations and updates \(X_{k+1}=X_k-a_k\widehat g_k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed two-evaluation SPSA recursion is recognizable, but no source is supplied and the perturbation assumptions needed to identify the standard family are not documented.

children.title: Adapted Recursive Processes
children.top_down_role: Recursive processes aligned with the available information history.

knowledge_statements.title: Adapted Recursive Processes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic recursions whose current state uses only currently available information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a filtered probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},\mathbb P)\), a recursive process \((X_k)\) is adapted if \(X_k\) is \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable for every \(k\). For a recursion \[X_{k+1}=\Phi_k(X_k,U_{k+1}),\] this requires \(X_k\) and all decisions used before observing \(U_{k+1}\) to be \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable, while \(X_{k+1}\) is \(\mathcal F_{k+1}\)-measurable. No update at time \(k\) may depend on information first revealed after time \(k+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adapted recursion uses only information available by the relevant iteration; each state is measurable with respect to the filtration at that time.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0}\) is a filtration on \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\).
\(\Phi_k\) is measurable on its stated domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_k\) is \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable for every \(k\ge0\).

notation.meaning: New information or noise used in the next update

children.title: Filtration Design
children.top_down_role: Information histories used to organize stochastic observations and iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Filtration Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information sets aligned with decision, sampling, and oracle-revelation times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a stochastic-approximation recursion, choose an increasing family \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0}\) so that \(\mathcal F_k\) contains the initialization and all samples, oracle outputs, and internal randomness revealed through iteration \(k\). The iterate \(X_k\), step size \(a_k\), and any sampling kernel selected before the next observation must be \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable. New noise \(M_{k+1}\) is analyzed conditionally on \(\mathcal F_k\), commonly through \(\mathbb E[M_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\). This timing convention makes predictability and conditional-noise assumptions mathematically testable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Design the filtration to contain exactly the revealed history, making current decisions measurable and the next noise analyzable conditionally on the past.
assumptions_latex: All random variables declared revealed by time \(k\) are \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Current decisions are \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable, and next-step noise conditions are stated relative to \(\mathcal F_k\).

notation.meaning: Sigma-algebra of information revealed by time k

children.title: Conditional Measurability
children.top_down_role: Measurability requirements relative to pre-update information.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Measurability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurability and conditional-moment predicates for stochastic-approximation updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X_{k+1}=X_k-a_k\bigl(h(X_k)+M_{k+1}\bigr)\), the conditional-information condition at time \(k\) is: \(X_k\) and \(a_k\) are \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable; \(M_{k+1}\) is \(\mathcal F_{k+1}\)-measurable and conditionally integrable; and \[\mathbb E[M_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\quad\text{almost surely}.\] If a conditional variance bound is required, additionally impose \(\mathbb E[\lVert M_{k+1}\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le C(1+\lVert X_k\rVert^2)\) almost surely for a deterministic \(C<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Current decisions must be measurable from the past, while next-step noise is newly measurable, conditionally integrable, and conditionally mean zero.
assumptions_latex: \(h(X_k)\) and \(M_{k+1}\) are well defined in the same finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[M_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\) almost surely, with the displayed conditional second-moment bound when required.

children.title: Anticipative-Information Failures
children.top_down_role: Invalid information-flow regimes involving unavailable future randomness.

knowledge_statements.title: Anticipative-Information Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete future-dependent noise choice that destroys conditional unbiasedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\xi_k)_{k\ge1}\) be independent Rademacher variables and let the natural past be \(\mathcal F_k=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_k)\). Define a purported step-size decision by \(a_k=1+\xi_{k+1}/2\), which uses unrevealed future noise, and take \(M_{k+1}=\xi_{k+1}\). Then \(a_k\) is not \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable and \[\mathbb E[a_kM_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=\mathbb E[\xi_{k+1}+1/2\mid\mathcal F_k]=1/2.\] Thus multiplying mean-zero noise by an anticipative decision produces a biased update increment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A step size chosen using the next noise value converts conditionally mean-zero noise into an increment with nonzero conditional mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_k\notin\mathcal F_k\) measurably and \(\mathbb E[a_kM_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=1/2\ne0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample calculation is correct, but it has no cited evidence. The conclusion should also say that a_k is not F_k-measurable rather than writing that a_k is not an element of F_k measurably.

children.title: Mean-Field Regularity
children.top_down_role: Continuity, local regularity, and growth families supporting limiting dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Mean-Field Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Lipschitz continuity and linear growth for finite-dimensional limiting dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mean field \(h:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) satisfies the standard local-regularity and growth condition if, for every \(R<\infty\), there exists \(L_R<\infty\) such that \[\lVert h(x)-h(y)\rVert\le L_R\lVert x-y\rVert\quad\text{whenever }\lVert x\rVert,\lVert y\rVert\le R,\] and there exists \(C<\infty\) such that \(\lVert h(x)\rVert\le C(1+\lVert x\rVert)\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R^d\). These conditions make the limiting differential equation \(\dot x=-h(x)\) locally well posed and exclude finite-time blow-up.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mean field is locally Lipschitz on every bounded set and grows at most linearly, supporting a well-defined limiting ordinary differential equation.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) is a deterministic map.
The ambient space carries the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The initial-value problem \(\dot x=-h(x)\), \(x(0)=x_0\), has a unique global solution for every \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant on the radius-R ball

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions and resulting global ODE conclusion are standard and fit the condition container, but the nontrivial global existence-and-uniqueness claim has no authoritative source locator.

children.title: Mean-Field Limit-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric conditions connecting mean-field dynamics with target solutions.

children.title: Mean-Field Equilibria
children.top_down_role: Stationary targets of the limiting mean-field dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Mean-Field Equilibria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equilibria of the autonomous differential inclusion associated with a stochastic-approximation mean field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H:\mathbb{R}^d\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^d\) be a set-valued mean field, and consider \(\dot x(t)\in-H(x(t))\). Its equilibrium set is
\[E_H:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:0\in H(x)\}.\]
Thus \(x^\star\) is an equilibrium exactly when the constant trajectory \(x(t)=x^\star\) satisfies the mean-field inclusion. For a single-valued field \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\), this reduces to \(E_h=\{x:h(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mean-field equilibrium is a zero of the drift operator, equivalently a point generating a constant trajectory of the limiting differential inclusion.

children.title: Solution-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Topological and metric structure of admissible target sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness and convexity properties of zeros arising from convex stochastic-optimization mean fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and suppose its minimizer set is nonempty. Then
\[S:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}F(x)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:0\in\partial F(x)\}\]
is a nonempty closed convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^d\). In particular, whenever the stochastic-approximation mean field is \(H=\partial F\), its solution set has this geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex objective with minimizers, the solution set equals the subdifferential zero set and is nonempty, closed, and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=(\partial F)^{-1}(0)\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

children.title: Attractor Geometry
children.top_down_role: Stable limiting regions of the associated dynamical system.

knowledge_statements.title: Attractor Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact attractors for the flow induced by a single-valued mean field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) generate a global flow \(\Phi_t\) through \(\dot x=-h(x)\). A nonempty compact set \(A\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is an attractor if it is invariant, \(\Phi_t(A)=A\) for every \(t\ge0\), and there exists an open neighborhood \(U\supset A\) such that
\[\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{x\in U}\operatorname{dist}(\Phi_t(x),A)=0.\]
Its basin is the set of initial points whose distance to \(A\) converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attractor is a compact invariant mean-field set that uniformly attracts every trajectory starting in some neighborhood; its basin contains all attracted initial states.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) generates a global continuous flow \((\Phi_t)_{t\ge0}\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is invariant and locally uniformly attracting under \(\Phi_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The flow-based attractor definition is mathematically coherent and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but the record has no citation. An authoritative dynamical-systems source with a specific definition, section, or page locator is required.

children.title: Equilibrium–Solution Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between dynamical equilibria and intended stochastic targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium–Solution Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex constrained correspondence for the projected mean-field differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}F\neq\varnothing\). Consider
\[\dot x(t)\in-\bigl(\partial F(x(t))+N_C(x(t))\bigr).\]
The equilibrium set is
\[E=\{x\in C:0\in\partial F(x)+N_C(x)\}.\]
Under the qualification \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}F)\cap\operatorname{ri}(C)\neq\varnothing\), one has \(E=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the convex qualification condition, equilibria of the constrained subgradient mean field are exactly the constrained minimizers of the objective.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}F(x)\).

children.title: Stochastic Error Compatibility Conditions

children.title: Stochastic Noise Control
children.top_down_role: Moment and dependence conditions governing random fluctuations.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Noise Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square-summable conditional-variance condition for martingale-difference noise in stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a filtration, let \(M_{n+1}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be \(\mathcal F_{n+1}\)-measurable, and let \(\alpha_n\ge0\) be \(\mathcal F_n\)-measurable. Stochastic noise is controlled when
\[\mathbb E[M_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=0,\qquad \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n^2\mathbb E[\|M_{n+1}\|^2\mid\mathcal F_n]<\infty\quad\text{a.s.}\]
Under these conditions, the weighted martingale series \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_nM_{n+1}\) converges almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Martingale-difference noise is compatible with stochastic approximation when its gain-weighted conditional variances are summable, ensuring convergence of the accumulated weighted noise.
assumptions_latex: \((M_{n+1})\) is square-integrable and adapted to \((\mathcal F_{n+1})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{n\ge0}\alpha_nM_{n+1}\) converges almost surely.

children.title: Systematic Bias Control
children.top_down_role: Admissible magnitude and decay regimes for systematic error.

knowledge_statements.title: Systematic Bias Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gain-weighted summability condition for predictable bias in a stochastic oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose an oracle error \(\xi_{n+1}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) is integrable and adapted to \((\mathcal F_{n+1})\). Define its predictable bias by
\[b_n:=\mathbb E[\xi_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n].\]
For nonnegative \(\mathcal F_n\)-measurable gains \(\alpha_n\), the bias is summably controlled if
\[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n\|b_n\|<\infty\quad\text{a.s.}\]
Consequently, the cumulative bias \(\sum_n\alpha_nb_n\) converges absolutely almost surely and cannot contribute an unbounded drift on the stochastic-approximation time scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Systematic oracle bias is controlled when its magnitude, weighted by the gains, is almost surely summable; the resulting cumulative bias is then finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{n\ge0}\alpha_nb_n\) converges absolutely almost surely.

children.title: Deterministic Perturbation Control
children.top_down_role: Admissible approximation or implementation disturbances.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Perturbation Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pathwise gain-weighted summability of deterministic or externally prescribed update errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((e_n)_{n\ge0}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be a deterministic perturbation sequence and let \((\alpha_n)_{n\ge0}\subset[0,\infty)\) be the gain sequence. The perturbation is summably controlled when
\[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n\|e_n\|<\infty.\]
Then \(\sum_n\alpha_ne_n\) converges absolutely. Moreover, for every \(T>0\),
\[\lim_{m\to\infty}\sup_{k\ge m:\,\sum_{n=m}^{k}\alpha_n\le T}\left\|\sum_{n=m}^{k}\alpha_ne_n\right\|=0,\]
so the perturbation vanishes on every bounded asymptotic-time window.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic update error is controlled when its gain-weighted norms are summable, which makes its contribution vanish on bounded asymptotic-time windows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_n\alpha_ne_n\) converges absolutely and its asymptotic-time window increments vanish.

children.title: Joint Error Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Combined regimes for random, systematic, and deterministic errors.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Error Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined martingale, predictable-bias, and deterministic-perturbation conditions for a stochastic-approximation recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Decompose an update error as \(\varepsilon_{n+1}=M_{n+1}+b_n+e_n\), where \(M_{n+1}\) is a martingale difference, \(b_n\) is predictable, and \(e_n\) is deterministic. For gains \(\alpha_n\ge0\), a sufficient joint compatibility condition is
\[\sum_n\alpha_n^2\mathbb E[\|M_{n+1}\|^2\mid\mathcal F_n]<\infty\quad\text{a.s.},\qquad
\sum_n\alpha_n\|b_n\|<\infty\quad\text{a.s.},\qquad
\sum_n\alpha_n\|e_n\|<\infty.\]
Then \(\sum_n\alpha_n\varepsilon_{n+1}\) converges almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The total weighted error converges when martingale variance is square-gain summable and both predictable bias and deterministic perturbations are gain-weighted summable.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[M_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=0\) and \(M_{n+1}\) is conditionally square-integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{n\ge0}\alpha_n\varepsilon_{n+1}\) converges almost surely.

children.title: Robbins–Monro Gain Conditions
children.top_down_role: Classical summability-based gain regimes for almost-sure convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Robbins–Monro Gain Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical nonsummable but square-summable positive gains for almost-sure stochastic-approximation convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A deterministic gain sequence \((\alpha_n)_{n\ge0}\) satisfies the classical Robbins–Monro conditions when
\[\alpha_n>0,\qquad \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n=\infty,\qquad \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n^2<\infty.\]
The first series supplies an infinite optimization-time horizon, while the second makes bounded-variance martingale noise square summable. These conditions imply \(\alpha_n\to0\), but that limit alone is not sufficient for the Robbins–Monro regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robbins–Monro gains are positive, have an infinite total sum, and have a finite squared sum; hence they vanish while retaining infinite cumulative optimization time.
assumptions_latex: \((\alpha_n)_{n\ge0}\) is a deterministic sequence of positive real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_n\alpha_n=\infty\), \(\sum_n\alpha_n^2<\infty\), and consequently \(\alpha_n\to0\).

notation.meaning: gain or step size at iteration n

children.title: Diminishing-Gain Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Diminishing policies organized by finite-time and asymptotic behavior.

children.title: Polynomial-Decay Gains
children.top_down_role: Diminishing gain schedules indexed by polynomial decay exponents.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Decay Gains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-law diminishing gains with a positive scale and optional iteration offset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For constants \(a>0\), \(n_0>0\), and \(\gamma>0\), a polynomial-decay gain sequence is
\[\alpha_n=\frac{a}{(n+n_0)^\gamma},\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.\]
It is positive, nonincreasing, and satisfies \(\alpha_n\to0\). Moreover, \(\sum_n\alpha_n=\infty\) exactly when \(\gamma\le1\), while \(\sum_n\alpha_n^2<\infty\) exactly when \(\gamma>1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial-decay gains follow a power law. They satisfy both Robbins–Monro summability requirements exactly when the exponent lies above one-half and at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\alpha_n)\) satisfies the Robbins–Monro conditions exactly when \(1/2<\gamma\le1\).

children.title: Harmonic Gains
children.top_down_role: Inverse-time gain schedules at the classical harmonic scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Harmonic Gains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reciprocal-linear gains, the endpoint polynomial regime with decay exponent one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For constants \(a>0\) and \(n_0>0\), the harmonic gain sequence is
\[\alpha_n=\frac{a}{n+n_0},\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.\]
It is the polynomial-decay family with exponent \(\gamma=1\). Hence \(\alpha_n\downarrow0\), \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n=\infty\), and \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\alpha_n^2<\infty\); therefore it satisfies the Robbins–Monro gain conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Harmonic gains decay reciprocally with iteration count and satisfy the Robbins–Monro requirements: their sum diverges while their squared sum converges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_n\to0\), \(\sum_n\alpha_n=\infty\), and \(\sum_n\alpha_n^2<\infty\).

children.title: Decay-Exponent Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavioral regimes determined by the polynomial decay exponent.

knowledge_statements.title: Decay-Exponent Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summability classification of power-law gains by their decay exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha_n=a(n+n_0)^{-\gamma}\) with \(a,n_0>0\) and \(\gamma>0\). Then the exponent partitions the gain regimes as follows:
\[0<\gamma\le\tfrac12:\ \sum_n\alpha_n=\infty,\ \sum_n\alpha_n^2=\infty;\]
\[\tfrac12<\gamma\le1:\ \sum_n\alpha_n=\infty,\ \sum_n\alpha_n^2<\infty;\]
\[\gamma>1:\ \sum_n\alpha_n<\infty,\ \sum_n\alpha_n^2<\infty.\]
Thus precisely the middle regime satisfies the classical Robbins–Monro conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power-law gains meet Robbins–Monro conditions only for exponents above one-half and at most one; slower decay accumulates excess noise, while faster decay has finite total gain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Robbins–Monro exponent range is \(1/2<\gamma\le1\).

children.title: Transient–Asymptotic Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tension between early progress, noise attenuation, and long-run behavior.

assumptions_latex: \((\xi_k)_{k\geq1}\) are independent with \(\mathbb E[\xi_k]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[\xi_k^2]=\sigma^2>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(2a\mu>1\), \(\mathbb E[e_k^2]=\Theta(k^{-2a\mu})e_0^2+\bigl(a^2\sigma^2/(2a\mu-1)+o(1)\bigr)k^{-1}\); the leading variance coefficient is minimized at \(a\mu=1\), rather than increasing throughout the admissible regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(e_{k+1}=(1-\mu\alpha_k)e_k-\alpha_k\xi_{k+1}\), where \(\alpha_k=a/(k+b)\), \(a,\mu>0\), \(b>a\mu\), \(e_0\in\mathbb R\) is deterministic, and the independent noises satisfy \(\mathbb E[\xi_k]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[\xi_k^2]=\sigma^2>0\). The squared deterministic transient is \(\Theta(k^{-2a\mu})e_0^2\). If \(2a\mu>1\), then \(\mathbb E[e_k^2]=\Theta(k^{-2a\mu})e_0^2+\bigl(a^2\sigma^2/(2a\mu-1)+o(1)\bigr)k^{-1}\). At \(2a\mu=1\), the noise contribution has order \((\log k)/k\), while for \(2a\mu<1\) it has order \(k^{-2a\mu}\). Increasing \(a\) accelerates deterministic bias decay, but the leading \(k^{-1}\) variance coefficient \(a^2\sigma^2/(2a\mu-1)\) decreases for \(1/2<a\mu<1\), is minimized at \(a\mu=1\), and increases for \(a\mu>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For harmonic gains on the scalar recursion, crossing the threshold 2a mu greater than 1 produces the inverse-iteration noise regime. A larger gain constant removes initial bias faster, but its leading variance coefficient is U-shaped and is minimized at a mu equal to 1.

children.title: Persistent-Gain Tracking Regimes
children.top_down_role: Persistent-gain dynamics for steady-state accuracy and changing-target tracking.

children.title: Constant-Gain Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Persistent-gain stochastic recursions and their long-run behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Gain Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearized constant-gain stochastic approximation near a stable equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha(H(x_k-x^\star)+\xi_{k+1})\), where \(H\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\), \(\alpha>0\), and \((\xi_k)\) is centered independent noise with covariance \(Q\). Writing \(e_k=x_k-x^\star\) and \(A=I-\alpha H\), the dynamics are \(e_{k+1}=Ae_k-\alpha\xi_{k+1}\). If \(\rho(A)<1\), then \(\mathbb E[e_k]=A^ke_0\) and the covariance satisfies \(P_{k+1}=AP_kA^\top+\alpha^2Q\). Consequently, \(P_k\) converges to the unique positive-semidefinite solution \(P_\alpha\) of \(P_\alpha=AP_\alpha A^\top+\alpha^2Q\), describing the invariant constant-gain fluctuation regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable constant-gain linear recursion forgets its mean geometrically while its covariance converges to the discrete Lyapunov solution associated with persistent noise.
assumptions_latex: \((\xi_k)\) are independent, centered, and have covariance \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[e_k]=A^ke_0\) and \(P_k\to P_\alpha\), where \(P_\alpha=AP_\alpha A^\top+\alpha^2Q\).

notation.meaning: constant-gain transition matrix I minus alpha H

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear mean and discrete-Lyapunov covariance statements are mathematically standard, and representation is an appropriate kind for this dynamics leaf. No citation is supplied for the invariant covariance claim, so source support is required.

children.title: Changing-Target Tracking
children.top_down_role: Response to objectives or equilibria that evolve over time.

knowledge_statements.title: Changing-Target Tracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-square tracking bound for a contractive noisy recursion with bounded target drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let target points \(x_k^\star\in\mathbb R^d\) satisfy \(\|x_{k+1}^\star-x_k^\star\|\leq\delta\), and let an adapted constant-gain recursion obey \(x_{k+1}-x_k^\star=T_k(x_k-x_k^\star)+\alpha\xi_{k+1}\), where \(\|T_kz\|\leq\rho\|z\|\), \(0\leq\rho<1\), and \(\mathbb E[\|\xi_{k+1}\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\leq\sigma^2\). For \(e_k=x_k-x_k^\star\), Minkowski's inequality gives \((\mathbb E\|e_k\|^2)^{1/2}\leq\rho^k\|e_0\|+(1-\rho^k)(\delta+\alpha\sigma)/(1-\rho)\). Thus persistent gain yields a bounded tracking neighborhood whenever contraction dominates target drift and noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contractive constant-gain recursion tracks a moving target within a neighborhood whose radius grows with target drift and oracle noise and shrinks with stronger contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathbb E\|e_k\|^2)^{1/2}\leq\rho^k\|e_0\|+(1-\rho^k)(\delta+\alpha\sigma)/(1-\rho)\).

notation.meaning: tracking error x_k minus x_k star

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed root-mean-square tracking bound follows from the stated contraction, drift, and conditional second-moment bounds, and property fits the leaf. A source with a specific dynamic-tracking locator is absent.

children.title: Stationary Error Floors
children.top_down_role: Terminal accuracy limits induced by persistent gains and noise.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Error Floors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact constant-gain error floor for a scalar noisy strongly convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(e_{k+1}=(1-\alpha\mu)e_k-\alpha\xi_{k+1}\), assume \(\mu>0\), \(0<\alpha\mu<2\), and independent noise with \(\mathbb E[\xi_k]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[\xi_k^2]=\sigma^2\). Then \(\mathbb E[e_k^2]=(1-\alpha\mu)^{2k}e_0^2+\alpha^2\sigma^2\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-\alpha\mu)^{2j}\). Hence \(\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbb E[e_k^2]=\alpha\sigma^2/(2\mu-\alpha\mu^2)\). In particular, nonzero constant gain and nonzero noise prevent mean-square convergence to the optimizer, while the stationary floor is \(\Theta(\alpha\sigma^2/\mu)\) as \(\alpha\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant gain under persistent gradient noise produces a nonzero stationary mean-square error, proportional to the gain for small gains.
assumptions_latex: \((\xi_k)\) are independent, centered, and have variance \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbb E[e_k^2]=\alpha\sigma^2/(2\mu-\alpha\mu^2)=\Theta(\alpha\sigma^2/\mu)\) as \(\alpha\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: scalar error relative to the optimizer

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Tracking–Variance Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Balance between responsiveness to drift and stochastic fluctuation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unconstrained balance is \(\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}\asymp(\delta/(\sigma\sqrt\mu))^{2/3}\), and it gives an upper-bound scale \(R(\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}})=O(\delta^{1/3}\sigma^{2/3}\mu^{-2/3})\); under the gain cap use \(\alpha=\min\{\bar\alpha,\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}\}\), up to constants depending on \(c_1,c_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small-gain upper-bound scaling law balancing moving-target lag against stochastic fluctuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a constant-gain tracker has steady-state root-mean-square error bounded by \(R(\alpha)\leq c_1\delta/(\mu\alpha)+c_2\sigma\sqrt{\alpha/\mu}\) for \(0<\alpha\leq\bar\alpha\), where \(c_1,c_2,\delta,\mu,\sigma,\bar\alpha>0\). The first term decreases and the second increases with \(\alpha\). Balancing the two terms without the cap gives \(\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}\asymp(\delta/(\sigma\sqrt\mu))^{2/3}\) and the upper-bound scale \(R(\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}})=O(\delta^{1/3}\sigma^{2/3}\mu^{-2/3})\), with constants depending on \(c_1,c_2\). Subject to the cap, use \(\alpha=\min\{\bar\alpha,\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}\}\), up to the same constant factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger gains reduce the lag term but increase the stochastic-fluctuation term. Balancing the displayed upper bound gives a two-thirds-power gain and an error upper bound proportional to delta to the one-third, sigma to the two-thirds, and mu to the negative two-thirds.

children.title: Stagewise Gain-Policy Family
children.top_down_role: Piecewise gain policies trading transient progress against stochastic error.

children.title: Staged Gain Policies
children.top_down_role: Piecewise-constant or piecewise-decaying gain regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Staged Gain Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-constant or piecewise-scheduled gains organized into predetermined stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an initial point \(x_0\in X\), a stochastic oracle \(G(x,\xi)\), stage boundaries \(0=t_0<t_1<t_2<\cdots\), and positive within-stage schedules \(\alpha_{s,j}\), set \(x^{(0)}_0=x_0\). For each stage \(s\geq0\), initialize \(x^{(s)}_0=x_{t_s}\) and perform \(x^{(s)}_{j+1}=\Pi_X(x^{(s)}_j-\alpha_{s,j}G(x^{(s)}_j,\xi_{t_s+j+1}))\) for \(0\leq j<t_{s+1}-t_s\). Set \(x_{t_{s+1}}=x^{(s)}_{t_{s+1}-t_s}\). A staged policy requires that every \(\alpha_{s,j}\) be fixed or predictable at its use; output may be the last iterate or a specified weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A staged policy partitions iterations into blocks and assigns each block its own predictable gain schedule, passing the terminal iterate to the next block.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(\alpha_{s,j}>0\) is fixed in advance or measurable before the corresponding oracle sample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated global gain is \(\alpha_k=\alpha_{s,k-t_s}\) for the unique stage satisfying \(t_s\leq k<t_{s+1}\).

notation.meaning: gain at local iteration j of stage s

children.title: Restarted Gain Policies
children.top_down_role: Gain schedules reset after selected progress or horizon events.

knowledge_statements.title: Restarted Gain Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagewise stochastic approximation that resets the local gain clock at each restart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given restart times \(0=t_0<t_1<t_2<\cdots\), base schedules \(a_s:\mathbb N_0\to(0,\infty)\), and \(x_0\in X\), define the stage index \(s(k)=\max\{s:t_s\leq k\}\) and local clock \(j(k)=k-t_{s(k)}\). At iteration \(k\), use \(\alpha_k=a_{s(k)}(j(k))\) and update \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_X(x_k-\alpha_kG(x_k,\xi_{k+1}))\). At \(k=t_s\), the local clock resets to zero, while the state is retained unless a separate state-reset map is specified. Stop at a prescribed budget or criterion and return the last iterate or a declared average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restarted policy preserves the current state but resets the gain schedule's local clock at designated restart times.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Restart times and gains are predictable with respect to the oracle filtration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k=a_{s(k)}(k-t_{s(k)})\), so each restart begins the selected base schedule again at local index zero.

notation.meaning: stage-s base gain at local time j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-clock reset construction matches the restarted-gain leaf and is properly classified as an algorithm. No inspectable citation supports this restart convention.

children.title: Stage-Transition Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural triggers governing movement between gain stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Stage-Transition Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predictability and termination requirements for data-dependent transitions between gain stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\geq0}\) be the stochastic-approximation filtration and let \(t_s\) denote the start of stage \(s\). A valid data-dependent transition time is an almost surely finite stopping time \(t_{s+1}>t_s\): for every \(k\), the event \(\{t_{s+1}\leq k\}\) belongs to \(\mathcal F_k\). Equivalently, a trigger may be written \(t_{s+1}=\inf\{k>t_s:C_s(k,\mathcal F_k)=1\}\), provided \(C_s\) uses only information available by iteration \(k\) and the infimum is almost surely finite. The next-stage gain parameters must be \(\mathcal F_{t_{s+1}}\)-measurable, preventing dependence on future oracle samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A data-dependent stage transition must be a finite stopping time, and the next stage's gains may depend only on information observed by that transition.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_k)\) contains all iterates and oracle observations available through iteration \(k\).
The trigger time satisfies \(t_{s+1}>t_s\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t_{s+1}\) is an almost surely finite \((\mathcal F_k)\)-stopping time and the next-stage parameters are \(\mathcal F_{t_{s+1}}\)-measurable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stopping-time and measurability requirements are mathematically appropriate transition conditions, and condition fits the terminal container. A specific source for data-dependent stage transitions is missing.

children.title: Restart Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Performance dependence on restart timing and reset scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of mean-square convergence under excessively frequent gain-clock restarts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(e_{k+1}=(1-\mu\alpha_k)e_k-\alpha_k\xi_{k+1}\), where \(\mu>0\), the independent noises are centered with variance \(\sigma^2>0\), and every stage restarts the schedule \(a(j)=a_0/(j+1)\). If all stage lengths are bounded by \(L<\infty\), then \(\alpha_k\geq a_0/L\) for every \(k\). Consequently, \(\mathbb E[e_{k+1}^2]\geq\alpha_k^2\sigma^2\geq a_0^2\sigma^2/L^2\), so the mean-square error cannot converge to zero. Thus convergence arguments requiring vanishing gains are sensitive to restart frequency: bounded stages destroy gain decay even though every isolated base schedule diminishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restarting a diminishing schedule too frequently can keep every realized gain bounded away from zero, creating a permanent noise floor and preventing mean-square convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(e_{k+1}=(1-\mu\alpha_k)e_k-\alpha_k\xi_{k+1}\) with independent centered noise of variance \(\sigma^2>0\).
Each stage uses \(a(j)=a_0/(j+1)\), and all stage lengths are at most \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_k\mathbb E[e_{k+1}^2]\geq a_0^2\sigma^2/L^2>0\), hence mean-square convergence fails.

notation.meaning: uniform upper bound on stage length

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct: bounded stage lengths keep the restarted harmonic gains uniformly positive, and independence makes the current noise contribution a positive lower bound on mean-square error. Failure_boundary is the correct kind, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Self-Tuning Gain-Policy Family
children.top_down_role: Self-tuning policies avoiding prior noise, curvature, or horizon calibration.

children.title: Adaptive Gain Calibration
children.top_down_role: Gain selection driven by observed optimization behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Gain Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predictable online calibration of gains from observed stochastic-gradient magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), \(x_0\in X\), calibration constants \(c>0\), \(v_0>0\), and bounds \(0<\alpha_{\min}\leq\alpha_{\max}\). After observing \(g_k=G(x_k,\xi_{k+1})\), update \(v_{k+1}=v_k+\|g_k\|^2\), set \(\alpha_{k+1}=\min\{\alpha_{\max},\max\{\alpha_{\min},c/\sqrt{v_{k+1}}\}\}\), and compute \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_X(x_k-\alpha_kg_k)\). Initialize \(\alpha_0\) from \(v_0\). The gain used with \(g_k\) is determined before that oracle sample, while the sample calibrates only subsequent gains. Output the final iterate or a declared weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive calibration updates a scale estimate from observed gradient magnitudes and uses it to choose the next predictable, clipped gain.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_{k+1}=\min\{\alpha_{\max},\max\{\alpha_{\min},c/\sqrt{v_0+\sum_{i=0}^k\|g_i\|^2}\}\}\) is adapted and uses no future oracle sample.

notation.meaning: stochastic gradient observed at iteration k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The update is a coherent predictable adaptive-gain algorithm, but it is a particular accumulated-squared-gradient or self-normalized construction and therefore overlaps the sibling Self-Normalized Gains container. A source is needed both for the algorithm and for its placement as adaptive calibration.

children.title: Parameter-Free Gains
children.top_down_role: Policies avoiding prior curvature or noise-scale calibration.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\geq0}\) describes the information available when \(\alpha_k\) is selected.
The nuisance-parameter set \(\Theta\) is declared explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(k\geq0\), \(\alpha_k\) is \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable and its defining map takes no element of \(\Theta\) as an input.

notation.meaning: declared collection of unavailable nuisance parameters
information available when gain alpha_k is selected
observed history available before selecting the kth gain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition relative to a declared class of unavailable problem parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an oracle filtration \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\geq0}\) and a declared nuisance-parameter set \(\Theta\), such as unavailable smoothness, strong-convexity, gradient, or noise bounds. Let \(h_k\) denote the observed history available before selecting the gain at iteration \(k\). A gain policy \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\) is parameter-free relative to \(\Theta\) if, for every \(k\geq0\), there is a measurable map \(\phi_k\) such that \(\alpha_k=\phi_k(h_k)\in(0,\infty)\), \(\alpha_k\) is \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable, and no \(\phi_k\) takes any element of \(\Theta\) as an input. User-specified geometry, units, confidence levels, and numerical safeguards must be declared separately; parameter-free does not mean free of all numerical constants. Dependence on a terminal horizon is a separate horizon-free property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gain policy is parameter-free relative to specified unavailable problem constants when each gain is selected measurably from observed history and declared safeguards without using those constants. Whether the policy also avoids the terminal horizon is a separate property.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Gains

children.title: Horizon-Free Schedules
children.top_down_role: Gain schedules that do not require a preset terminal horizon.

assumptions_latex: For each \(k\geq0\), \(h_k\) contains exactly the information available when the gain at iteration \(k\) is selected.
Each selected gain is positive and measurable with respect to the information represented by \(h_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(H_1<H_2\) and every common history prefix \((h_0,\ldots,h_{H_1-1})\), \(\alpha_k^{(H_1)}=\alpha_k^{(H_2)}\) for all \(0\leq k<H_1\).

notation.meaning: finite terminal iteration or run horizon
gain at iteration k in a run declared with horizon H
observed history available when the kth gain is selected
decay exponent in the deterministic example

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anytime gain policies whose rules and realized prefixes do not depend on the eventual stopping horizon.

source_refs.locator: 8.3 The Stochastic Projected Subgradient Method p. 221
source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each finite horizon \(H\in\mathbb N\), let \(\alpha_k^{(H)}\) denote the gain used at iteration \(k<H\), and let \(h_k\) denote the observed history available when that gain is selected. The policy is horizon-free if there exist measurable maps \((\phi_k)_{k\geq0}\), none depending on \(H\), such that \(\alpha_k^{(H)}=\phi_k(h_k)>0\) for every \(H\) and every \(k<H\). Equivalently, for any \(H_1<H_2\), two runs presented with the same history through iteration \(H_1-1\) use the same gains through that iteration. Thus stopping or extending a run does not retroactively alter earlier gain rules. A deterministic example is \(\alpha_k=c/(k+b)^p\), where \(c,b>0\) and \(p\in(0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A horizon-free policy uses gain-selection rules that do not take the eventual run length as input. Runs with the same observed history therefore have identical gain prefixes regardless of when they are stopped or extended.

children.title: Self-Normalized Gains
children.top_down_role: Gain scales determined by accumulated stochastic first-order information.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Normalized Gains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-norm normalization for stochastic approximation with data-dependent, horizon-free gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an initial point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), constants \(\gamma>0\) and \(\delta>0\), and stochastic directions \(G_n\), set \(S_{-1}=\delta\). For \(n\geq0\), observe \(G_n\), update \(S_n=S_{n-1}+\lVert G_n\rVert^2\), choose the self-normalized gain \(a_n=\gamma S_n^{-1/2}\), and form \(x_{n+1}=x_n-a_nG_n\). For a closed convex feasible set \(C\), replace the last update by \(x_{n+1}=\Pi_C(x_n-a_nG_n)\). After \(N\) updates, output either \(x_N\) or a specified weighted average of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accumulate squared stochastic-direction norms and scale each update by the inverse square root of that accumulated magnitude, optionally projecting onto a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_n=\gamma\bigl(\delta+\sum_{k=0}^n\lVert G_k\rVert^2\bigr)^{-1/2}\) defines a nonincreasing, data-dependent gain sequence.

notation.meaning: stochastic search direction at iteration n

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but no citation supports this exact cumulative squared-norm gain, its timing convention, or the optional projected variant.

children.title: Lyapunov-Drift Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Stability through coercive energy and drift constructions.

children.title: Lyapunov Stability Certificates
children.top_down_role: Energy-based structures used to establish stochastic stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Lyapunov Stability Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A discrete conditional-drift certificate for almost-sure boundedness of stochastic-approximation iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x_n,\mathcal F_n)\) be adapted and let \(V:\mathbb{R}^d\to[0,\infty)\) be coercive. Suppose predictable sequences \(a_n,b_n\geq0\) and a measurable \(W\geq0\) satisfy \(\sum_n b_n<\infty\) almost surely and \[\mathbb E[V(x_{n+1})\mid\mathcal F_n]\leq V(x_n)-a_nW(x_n)+b_n.\] Then the almost-supermartingale conclusion gives finite almost-sure convergence of \(V(x_n)\) and \(\sum_n a_nW(x_n)<\infty\). Consequently \(\sup_nV(x_n)<\infty\), and coercivity certifies \(\sup_n\lVert x_n\rVert<\infty\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coercive nonnegative Lyapunov function with summably perturbed negative conditional drift certifies bounded iterates and finite accumulated dissipation almost surely.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional-drift inequality holds almost surely for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(x_n)\) converges finitely, \(\sum_n a_nW(x_n)<\infty\), and \(\sup_n\lVert x_n\rVert<\infty\) almost surely.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits, but an authoritative almost-supermartingale source is required to verify the necessary integrability and measurability hypotheses for the asserted convergence and dissipation conclusions.

children.title: Negative-Drift Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regions where expected motion favors lower Lyapunov levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Drift Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional Lyapunov drift outside a stability region, allowing summable perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an adapted recursion \((x_n,\mathcal F_n)\), a Lyapunov function \(V\geq0\), a measurable dissipation function \(W\geq0\), and a measurable stability region \(K\), a negative-drift regime holds when predictable \(a_n,b_n\geq0\) satisfy \[\mathbb E[V(x_{n+1})-V(x_n)\mid\mathcal F_n]\leq-a_nW(x_n)\mathbf 1_{\{x_n\notin K\}}+b_n\] almost surely, with \(\sum_n b_n<\infty\). A strict regime additionally requires \(\inf_{x\notin K}W(x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside a designated stability region, expected Lyapunov change is negative up to a summable error; strict drift has uniformly positive dissipation there.
assumptions_latex: \((x_n,\mathcal F_n)\) is adapted and \(V,W\) are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequality defines a negative-drift regime; it is strict if \(\inf_{x\notin K}W(x)>0\).

notation.meaning: region inside which strict drift need not hold

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the negative-drift leaf, but the exact predictable, summable-remainder, and strict-dissipation formulation has no cited source.

children.title: Coercive Stability Geometry
children.top_down_role: Large-scale energy geometry supporting bounded stochastic trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Stability Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-sublevel geometry converting a Lyapunov bound into an iterate bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V:\mathbb{R}^d\to[0,\infty)\) be lower semicontinuous and coercive, meaning \(V(x)\to\infty\) whenever \(\lVert x\rVert\to\infty\). Then every sublevel set \(L_c=\{x:V(x)\leq c\}\) is compact. Hence, on any sample path for which \(\sup_nV(x_n)=c<\infty\), all iterates belong to the compact set \(L_c\), so \(\sup_n\lVert x_n\rVert<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-semicontinuous coercive Lyapunov function has compact sublevels, so bounded Lyapunov values force bounded iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(c<\infty\), \(L_c\) is compact, and \(\sup_nV(x_n)<\infty\) implies \(\sup_n\lVert x_n\rVert<\infty\).

notation.meaning: c-sublevel set of the Lyapunov function

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically standard and matches the leaf, but standard-field rationale does not replace the required inspectable citation and locator.

children.title: Drift-Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regions where stabilizing drift becomes too weak or changes direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Drift-Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-walk counterexample showing that nonnegative Lyapunov drift does not certify boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_0=0\) and \(x_{n+1}=x_n+\xi_{n+1}\), where \((\xi_n)\) are independent with \(\mathbb P(\xi_n=1)=\mathbb P(\xi_n=-1)=1/2\), and take \(V(x)=x^2\). Then \[\mathbb E[V(x_{n+1})-V(x_n)\mid\mathcal F_n]=1.\] Thus no negative-drift inequality with summable positive remainder can hold outside a compact set for this \(V\). The one-dimensional simple symmetric random walk is almost surely unbounded, so coercivity of \(V\) alone does not supply a stability certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric random walk has coercive quadratic Lyapunov function but positive unit drift and is almost surely unbounded, exposing the boundary of drift-based stability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[V(x_{n+1})-V(x_n)\mid\mathcal F_n]=1\) and \(\sup_n|x_n|=\infty\) almost surely.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample fits the failure-boundary leaf and its drift computation is coherent, but the almost-sure unboundedness claim and resulting impossibility statement require a source.

children.title: Explicit Recursion Stabilization Family
children.top_down_role: Explicit mechanisms for controlling unbounded recursions.

children.title: Projected Stabilization
children.top_down_role: Iterate control through restriction to a prescribed feasible region.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Stabilization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection stabilizes stochastic approximation within a prescribed closed convex region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), initialize \(x_0\in C\). For \(n\geq0\), obtain a stochastic direction \(G_n\), choose a gain \(a_n>0\), and update \[x_{n+1}=\Pi_C(x_n-a_nG_n),\qquad \Pi_C(y)=\mathop{\rm argmin}_{z\in C}\lVert z-y\rVert.\] Stop according to a prescribed iteration or accuracy rule and output the final iterate or a specified average. The projection guarantees \(x_n\in C\) for every \(n\), and therefore boundedness whenever \(C\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project every stochastic update onto a closed convex region; feasibility is invariant, and a bounded region directly stabilizes all iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_n\in C\) for all \(n\); if \(C\) is bounded, then \(\sup_n\lVert x_n\rVert<\infty\).

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization
source_refs.locator: 8.3 The Stochastic Projected Subgradient Method p. 221
