children.title: Truncated Recursions
children.top_down_role: Recursion control through rejection, clipping, or reset mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Truncated Recursions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reset-based truncation prevents accepted stochastic-approximation iterates from leaving prescribed regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((K_j)_{j\geq0}\) be closed truncation regions, let \(r_j\in K_j\) be reset points, and initialize \(x_0\in K_0\), \(\sigma_0=0\). At iteration \(n\), form \(y_{n+1}=x_n+a_nH(x_n,\xi_{n+1})\). If \(y_{n+1}\in K_{\sigma_n}\), set \((x_{n+1},\sigma_{n+1})=(y_{n+1},\sigma_n)\); otherwise set \((x_{n+1},\sigma_{n+1})=(r_{\sigma_n+1},\sigma_n+1)\). After the stopping index, output \(x_n\) together with the truncation count \(\sigma_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a proposed stochastic-approximation step inside the active region; otherwise reset to a safe point and advance the truncation index.
assumptions_latex: \(K_j\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is closed and \(r_j\in K_j\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted iterate lies in its active region, while \(\sigma_n\) records the number of rejected proposals.

notation.meaning: safe reset point for region j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reset-based algorithm fits the leaf, but no citation establishes this exact truncation-index and reset-point convention.

children.title: Expanding-Region Stabilization
children.top_down_role: Iterate control through a sequence of progressively larger regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Expanding-Region Stabilization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncation with nested regions whose union covers the state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose compact sets \(K_0\subseteq K_1\subseteq\cdots\) with \(K_j\subseteq\operatorname{int}K_{j+1}\) and \(\bigcup_{j\geq0}K_j=\mathbb{R}^d\), together with reset points \(r_j\in K_j\). Initialize \((x_0,\sigma_0)=(r_0,0)\). Given \(y_{n+1}=x_n+a_nH(x_n,\xi_{n+1})\), accept it without changing \(\sigma_n\) when \(y_{n+1}\in K_{\sigma_n}\); otherwise set \(x_{n+1}=r_{\sigma_n+1}\) and \(\sigma_{n+1}=\sigma_n+1\). Output the terminal iterate and truncation count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use nested compact acceptance regions; each rejected proposal triggers a reset and enlarges the active region, eventually admitting every fixed bounded subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every bounded \(B\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), there exists \(j_B\) such that \(B\subseteq K_j\) for all \(j\geq j_B\).

notation.meaning: reset point in the j-th region

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expanding-region algorithm and exhaustion conclusion are coherent, but the specific nested-region truncation scheme lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Stabilization-Induced Bias
children.top_down_role: Target distortion introduced by active iterate-control mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Stabilization-Induced Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-mean bias introduced by projecting or truncating an otherwise unbiased stochastic update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the unstabilized proposal be \(y_{n+1}=x_n-a_nG_n\), where \(\mathbb E[G_n\mid\mathcal F_n]=g(x_n)\), and let a measurable stabilizer \(S_n\) produce \(x_{n+1}=S_n(y_{n+1})\). Define \[b_n^{\mathrm{stab}}=a_n^{-1}\mathbb E[S_n(y_{n+1})-y_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n].\] Then the stabilized conditional mean increment has the exact representation \[\mathbb E[x_{n+1}-x_n\mid\mathcal F_n]=-a_ng(x_n)+a_nb_n^{\mathrm{stab}}.\] Thus stabilization is conditionally unbiased precisely when \(b_n^{\mathrm{stab}}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conditional mean correction caused by projection, truncation, or resetting is an additive drift bias equal to the expected stabilization displacement divided by the gain.
assumptions_latex: \(a_n>0\), and \(x_n,G_n\) are integrable as required by the displayed expectations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[x_{n+1}-x_n\mid\mathcal F_n]=-a_ng(x_n)+a_nb_n^{\mathrm{stab}}\), with zero stabilization bias exactly when \(b_n^{\mathrm{stab}}=0\).

notation.meaning: conditional drift bias induced by stabilization
conditional mean of the unstabilized direction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact conditional-mean decomposition fits the stabilization-bias leaf, but no source supports this definition and its interpretation for projection, truncation, and resetting.

children.title: Large-Scale ODE Stability Calculus
children.top_down_role: Stability inferred from limiting behavior at large iterate scale.

children.title: Scaled-Limit Criteria
children.top_down_role: Large-radius rescaling structures used to assess trajectory control.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled-Limit Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Borkar–Meyn-type scaling conditions for stability of stochastic-approximation recursions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a drift \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\), define \(h_c(x)=h(cx)/c\) for \(c\geq1\). The scaled-limit criterion holds if a locally Lipschitz map \(h_\infty\) exists such that \(h_c\to h_\infty\) uniformly on every compact subset of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and the origin is a globally asymptotically stable equilibrium of \(\dot z=h_\infty(z)\). For a stochastic recursion, this criterion must be paired with standard gain, martingale-noise, and drift-regularity hypotheses before it yields almost-sure iterate boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescale the drift at increasing radii; require compact-uniform convergence to a limiting drift whose ODE has a globally asymptotically stable origin.
assumptions_latex: \(h_c\) converges uniformly on compact sets to a locally Lipschitz \(h_\infty\).
The origin is globally asymptotically stable for \(\dot z=h_\infty(z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((h,h_\infty)\) satisfies the scaled-limit stability criterion.

notation.meaning: drift observed at spatial scale c

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the scaled-limit leaf and appropriately avoids claiming boundedness by itself, but the precise scaling convergence and limiting-ODE requirements need an authoritative Borkar–Meyn-type locator.

children.title: Limiting ODE Stability
children.top_down_role: Stability properties of the dynamical system induced at large scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting ODE Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global asymptotic stability condition for the ODE governing the drift at infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_\infty:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be locally Lipschitz with \(h_\infty(0)=0\), and let \(\phi(t,z_0)\) denote the unique maximal solution of \(\dot z=h_\infty(z)\), \(z(0)=z_0\). The limiting ODE has a globally asymptotically stable origin when every solution exists for all \(t\geq0\), the origin is Lyapunov stable, and \(\lim_{t\to\infty}\phi(t,z_0)=0\) for every \(z_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting ODE is stable when all forward solutions exist, nearby states remain nearby, and every initial state converges to the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\) is globally asymptotically stable exactly when it is Lyapunov stable, all forward solutions are global, and \(\phi(t,z_0)\to0\) for every \(z_0\).

notation.meaning: ODE solution at time t from initial state z_0

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global asymptotic stability condition is standard, precise, and appropriate for the leaf, but no authoritative section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Large-Radius Drift Geometry
children.top_down_role: Directional behavior of the mean field far from bounded regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Radius Drift Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform radial inward drift outside a ball as a large-scale stability condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be locally Lipschitz. A quadratic large-radius inward-drift condition holds if constants \(R\geq0\) and \(\mu>0\) satisfy \[\langle x,h(x)\rangle\leq-\mu\lVert x\rVert^2\qquad\text{whenever }\lVert x\rVert\geq R.\] Along any solution of \(\dot z=h(z)\) lying outside the radius-\(R\) ball, \[\frac{d}{dt}\frac12\lVert z(t)\rVert^2\leq-\mu\lVert z(t)\rVert^2.\] Hence the squared radius decreases strictly until the trajectory reaches that ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the drift has a uniformly negative radial component beyond a fixed radius, ODE trajectories contract toward that radius at a quadratic rate.
assumptions_latex: There exist \(R\geq0\) and \(\mu>0\) satisfying the displayed radial inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: While \(\lVert z(t)\rVert\geq R\), \(\frac{d}{dt}\lVert z(t)\rVert^2\leq-2\mu\lVert z(t)\rVert^2\).

notation.meaning: radius beyond which inward drift is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The radial drift condition and differential inequality are mathematically coherent and match the leaf, but the record lacks the required inspectable citation.

children.title: Unstable Scaled Limits
children.top_down_role: Large-scale limiting dynamics incompatible with iterate boundedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Scaled Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the large-scale ODE criterion to certify bounded stochastic-approximation iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the recursion \(x_{n+1}=x_n+a_n(h(x_n)+M_{n+1})\) and the scaled fields \(h_c(x)=h(cx)/c\). Suppose that, along some sequence \(c_k\to\infty\), the fields \(h_{c_k}\) converge uniformly on compact sets to \(h_\infty\). If the limiting ODE \(\dot x=h_\infty(x)\) has a solution starting on the unit sphere that does not enter any fixed ball \(B_\rho(0)\), with \(0<\rho<1\), within a common finite time, then the usual scaled-ODE contraction argument fails. Consequently, this scaled limit alone supplies no boundedness certificate for \((x_n)\); additional drift, Lyapunov, projection, or coercivity assumptions are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a scaled limiting ODE does not contract unit-scale states toward the origin, the standard large-radius rescaling argument cannot certify bounded stochastic-approximation iterates.
assumptions_latex: \(h_{c_k}\to h_\infty\) uniformly on compact subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\)
\(\exists x_0,\ \lVert x_0\rVert=1\), whose limiting-ODE trajectory lacks the stated uniform contraction
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled-limit stability criterion does not imply \(\sup_n\lVert x_n\rVert<\infty\).

notation.meaning: mean field viewed at spatial scale c
open Euclidean ball of radius rho centered at zero

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between failure of a sufficient scaled-ODE certificate and actual iterate instability is appropriate, but the required uniform trajectory and time quantifiers are unclear and no authoritative scaled-ODE locator is supplied.

children.title: Robbins–Siegmund Convergence Principle
children.top_down_role: The almost-supermartingale organizer for stochastic descent, summability, and trajectory convergence.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications

children.title: Almost-Supermartingale Arguments
children.top_down_role: Conditional descent processes with controlled perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Supermartingale Arguments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robbins–Siegmund convergence principle for nonnegative adapted processes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_n)\) be a filtration. Let \((V_n)\) be a sequence of nonnegative, integrable, \(\mathcal F_n\)-adapted random variables, and let \((U_n)\), \((A_n)\), and \((B_n)\) be nonnegative \(\mathcal F_n\)-adapted random variables. Assume almost surely that \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}A_n<\infty\), \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}B_n<\infty\), and \[\mathbb E[V_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\leq (1+A_n)V_n-U_n+B_n\quad\text{for every }n.\] Then \((V_n)\) converges almost surely to a finite random variable and \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}U_n<\infty\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integrable nonnegative adapted process, conditional descent with summable multiplicative and additive errors forces convergence to a finite limit and finite accumulated descent almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \(V_n\) is nonnegative, integrable, and \(\mathcal F_n\)-adapted; \(U_n,A_n,B_n\geq0\) are \(\mathcal F_n\)-adapted
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_n\to V_\infty<\infty\) and \(\sum_nU_n<\infty\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: nonnegative integrable Lyapunov or error process

children.title: Stochastic Quasi-Fejér Arguments
children.top_down_role: Distance-based stochastic convergence mechanisms for solution sets and fixed points.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Quasi-Fejér Arguments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional distance descent relative to a nonempty closed solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonempty closed subset of a Hilbert space \(H\), and let \((x_n)\) be adapted to \((\mathcal F_n)\), with \(\mathbb E\lVert x_n-s\rVert^2<\infty\) for every \(n\) and every fixed \(s\in S\). Suppose that, for every fixed \(s\in S\), there are nonnegative adapted processes \((\alpha_n)\), \((\beta_n(s))\), and \((\delta_n)\) such that \[\mathbb E[\lVert x_{n+1}-s\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_n]\leq(1+\alpha_n)\lVert x_n-s\rVert^2-\delta_n+\beta_n(s),\] where \(\sum_n\alpha_n<\infty\) and \(\sum_n\beta_n(s)<\infty\) almost surely. Then, for each fixed \(s\in S\), \(\lVert x_n-s\rVert^2\) converges almost surely, and \(\sum_n\delta_n<\infty\) almost surely. Additional limit-set assumptions are required to conclude that \((x_n)\) converges to a point of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each fixed target point, a conditional quasi-Fejér inequality makes the squared distance converge almost surely and makes accumulated descent finite; identifying a limit in the target set requires additional assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(x_n\) is \(\mathcal F_n\)-adapted and \(\mathbb E\lVert x_n-s\rVert^2<\infty\) for every \(n\) and fixed \(s\in S\)
For each fixed \(s\in S\), the displayed inequality holds and \(\sum_n\alpha_n<\infty\), \(\sum_n\beta_n(s)<\infty\) almost surely
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each fixed \(s\in S\), \(\lVert x_n-s\rVert^2\) converges almost surely, and \(\sum_n\delta_n<\infty\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: summable additive perturbation for the fixed reference point s

children.title: Descent-to-Limit Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Passage from accumulated descent control to admissible stochastic limits.

children.title: Accumulated Descent Control
children.top_down_role: Long-run control obtained from cumulative stochastic descent.

knowledge_statements.title: Accumulated Descent Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summability consequence of a Robbins–Siegmund conditional-descent inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((V_n)\) be nonnegative, integrable, and adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal F_n)\), and let \((D_n)\) and \((E_n)\) be nonnegative adapted processes. If \[\mathbb E[V_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\leq V_n-D_n+E_n\] and \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E_n<\infty\) almost surely, then \[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}D_n<\infty\quad\text{almost surely}.\] Hence, if \(D_n=a_nr_n\) with \(a_n,r_n\geq0\), then \(\sum_na_nr_n<\infty\) almost surely. This weighted summability alone does not imply \(r_n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A summably perturbed conditional descent inequality for an integrable Lyapunov process makes total descent finite. Weighted residual summability follows, but residual convergence requires additional assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(V_n\geq0\) is integrable and \(\mathcal F_n\)-adapted; \(D_n,E_n\geq0\) are \(\mathcal F_n\)-adapted
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_nD_n<\infty\) almost surely; if \(D_n=a_nr_n\), then \(\sum_na_nr_n<\infty\) almost surely.

children.title: Summable Residual Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where stationarity or feasibility residuals have finite accumulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Summable Residual Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions converting weighted residual summability into vanishing residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((a_n)\) and \((r_n)\) be nonnegative sequences satisfying \(\sum_na_n=\infty\) and \(\sum_na_nr_n<\infty\). Then \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}r_n=0\). Moreover, assume the following persistence condition: for every \(\varepsilon>0\), if \(r_n\geq2\varepsilon\) for infinitely many \(n\), then there exist \(c_\varepsilon>0\) and infinitely many pairwise disjoint finite integer intervals \(I_j\) such that each \(I_j\) contains an index \(n_j\) with \(r_{n_j}\geq2\varepsilon\), while \(r_k\geq\varepsilon\) for every \(k\in I_j\) and \(\sum_{k\in I_j}a_k\geq c_\varepsilon\). Under this additional condition, \(r_n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted residual summability with divergent total weight implies zero lower limit. If every recurring residual spike persists over a uniformly positive amount of weight, then the residual converges to zero.
assumptions_latex: The stated positive-weight persistence condition holds when full convergence is asserted
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}r_n=0\); under the persistence condition, \(r_n\to0\).

notation.meaning: a finite persistence interval associated with a residual spike

children.title: Stochastic Limit Identification
children.top_down_role: Classification of possible limits using accumulated descent information.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Limit Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional stochastic quasi-Fejér limit identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subset\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty and closed, and let \((x_n)\) be a sequence of \(\mathbb R^d\)-valued random vectors. Suppose there is an event \(\Omega_0\) of probability one such that, for every \(\omega\in\Omega_0\), the sequence \((x_n(\omega))\) is bounded, \(\lVert x_n(\omega)-s\rVert\) converges for every \(s\in S\), and every cluster point of \((x_n(\omega))\) belongs to \(S\). Then there exists an \(S\)-valued random vector \(x_\infty\) such that \(x_n\to x_\infty\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, if boundedness, convergence of all distances to the target, and admissibility of every cluster point hold on one full-probability event, the random sequence converges almost surely to one target point.
assumptions_latex: On one event \(\Omega_0\) with \(\mathbb P(\Omega_0)=1\), \((x_n)\) is bounded and \(\lVert x_n-s\rVert\) converges for every \(s\in S\)
On the same event \(\Omega_0\), every cluster point of \((x_n)\) lies in \(S\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an \(S\)-valued random vector \(x_\infty\) such that \(x_n\to x_\infty\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: common event on which all pathwise assumptions hold

children.title: Cluster-Point Admissibility
children.top_down_role: Conditions placing stochastic cluster points in the intended target set.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-Point Admissibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual certificate placing all finite-dimensional cluster points in the target set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)\) be continuous and let \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:R(x)=0\}\). If a sequence \((x_n)\subset\mathbb R^d\) satisfies \(R(x_n)\to0\), then every cluster point \(\bar x\) of \((x_n)\) belongs to \(S\). In particular, when \((x_n)\) is bounded, the vanishing residual certifies that all of its nonempty collection of cluster points is admissible. The same statement holds pathwise for a stochastic sequence on any event where residual convergence holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous residual whose zero set is the target certifies that every cluster point is admissible whenever the residual vanishes; boundedness additionally guarantees the existence of cluster points in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every cluster point \(\bar x\) of \((x_n)\) satisfies \(\bar x\in S\); if \((x_n)\) is bounded, at least one such cluster point exists.

children.title: ODE Method
children.top_down_role: Interpolated-trajectory analysis through limiting ordinary differential equations.

knowledge_statements.title: ODE Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic-pseudotrajectory form of the ODE method for bounded stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(x_{n+1}=x_n+a_n(h(x_n)+M_{n+1}+e_n)\) in \(\mathbb R^d\). Assume that \(h\) is locally Lipschitz, \(a_n>0\), \(a_n\to0\), \(\sum_na_n=\infty\), and the iterates are almost surely bounded. If, on every bounded continuous-time window, the accumulated interpolated noise and error vanish asymptotically, then the affine interpolation \(X(t)\), defined at times \(t_n=\sum_{k<n}a_k\), is almost surely an asymptotic pseudotrajectory of the flow generated by \(\dot x=h(x)\). Consequently, its compact limit set is invariant and internally chain transitive for that flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under boundedness and vanishing accumulated perturbations, the interpolated stochastic-approximation path asymptotically follows the mean ODE, and its limit set is invariant and internally chain transitive.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) is locally Lipschitz and \((x_n)\) is almost surely bounded
Accumulated \(M_{n+1}+e_n\) vanishes uniformly on each bounded interpolated-time window
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\) is an asymptotic pseudotrajectory of \(\dot x=h(x)\), and its limit set is compact, invariant, and internally chain transitive almost surely.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A theorem is an appropriate role for this formal ODE-method result, but the phrase describing vanishing accumulated perturbations does not define its quantifiers or interpolation indices. An authoritative ODE-method theorem locator is required before fixing the hypotheses and conclusion.

children.title: Differential-Inclusion Method
children.top_down_role: Set-valued limiting dynamics for nonsmooth or discontinuous mean fields.

knowledge_statements.title: Differential-Inclusion Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued dynamical method for bounded stochastic approximation with nonsmooth mean fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(x_{n+1}=x_n+a_n(v_n+M_{n+1}+e_n)\), where \(v_n\in F(x_n)\) and \(F:\mathbb R^d\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^d\) is a Marchaud map: its values are nonempty, compact, and convex; its graph is closed; and it has linear growth. Assume \(a_n\to0\), \(\sum_na_n=\infty\), the iterates are almost surely bounded, and accumulated perturbations vanish on bounded interpolated-time windows. Then the affine interpolation is almost surely a perturbed solution, hence an asymptotic pseudotrajectory, of
\[\dot x(t)\in F(x(t)).\]
Its compact limit set is invariant in the set-valued sense and internally chain transitive for the induced semiflow relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a Marchaud mean-field map and negligible accumulated perturbations, interpolation follows a differential inclusion whose compact limit set is invariant and internally chain transitive.
assumptions_latex: \(a_n>0,\ a_n\to0,\ \sum_na_n=\infty\), and \((x_n)\) is almost surely bounded
Accumulated perturbations vanish on bounded interpolated-time windows
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interpolation asymptotically follows \(\dot x\in F(x)\), and its limit set is compact, invariant, and internally chain transitive almost surely.

notation.meaning: selected mean-field direction at iteration n

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the method container, but the transition from the discrete inclusion to a perturbed solution or asymptotic pseudotrajectory, and the precise set-valued invariance and chain-transitivity conclusion, depend on source-specific definitions not provided here.

children.title: Dynamical Limit-Set Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Geometric classification of stochastic-approximation limit sets.

children.title: Invariant Limit Sets
children.top_down_role: Limit regions preserved by the associated dynamical system.

knowledge_statements.title: Invariant Limit Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant compact sets for continuous-time limiting dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi:[0,\infty)\times X\to X\) be a continuous semiflow on a metric space \(X\). A nonempty compact set \(L\subset X\) is invariant if
\[\Phi_t(L)=L\quad\text{for every }t\ge0,\]
where \(\Phi_t(x)=\Phi(t,x)\). For a differential inclusion, invariance means that for every \(x\in L\) there exists a complete solution \(z:\mathbb R\to L\) with \(z(0)=x\) that remains in \(L\) for all time. If a precompact trajectory has an omega-limit set and is an asymptotic pseudotrajectory, that omega-limit set is invariant under the corresponding limiting dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invariant limit set is compact, nonempty, and preserved by the limiting flow; for an inclusion, every point lies on a complete trajectory contained in the set.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is a continuous semiflow on a metric space \(X\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\) is invariant exactly when \(\Phi_t(L)=L\) for every \(t\ge0\), with the stated complete-solution interpretation for inclusions.

notation.meaning: time-t map of the limiting semiflow
complete solution of a differential inclusion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but the record combines strong semiflow invariance, a differential-inclusion complete-solution notion, and an asymptotic-pseudotrajectory theorem. These notions vary in the literature and require separate authoritative locators.

children.title: Attractor Limit Sets
children.top_down_role: Stable limiting regions that capture nearby trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Attractor Limit Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact invariant sets that uniformly attract a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi\) be a continuous semiflow on a metric space \((X,d)\). A nonempty compact invariant set \(A\subset X\) is an attractor if there exists an open neighborhood \(U\supset A\) such that
\[\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{x\in U} d(\Phi_t(x),A)=0,\qquad d(y,A)=\inf_{a\in A}d(y,a).\]
The basin of attraction is
\[B(A)=\{x\in X:d(\Phi_t(x),A)\to0\text{ as }t\to\infty\}.\]
A trajectory whose tail eventually remains in a compact subset of \(B(A)\) has omega-limit set contained in \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attractor is a compact invariant set uniformly approached from some neighborhood; trajectories eventually confined within its basin have limit sets contained in the attractor.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is a continuous semiflow on the metric space \((X,d)\)
\(A\subset X\) is nonempty, compact, and invariant
An open neighborhood \(U\supset A\) satisfies the displayed uniform-attraction condition
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is an attractor with basin \(B(A)\); compactly basin-confined trajectory tails have omega-limit sets contained in \(A\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but uniform attraction of an entire open neighborhood is stronger than some standard attractor definitions, and the additional omega-limit assertion needs its own hypotheses. A specific dynamical-systems source is required.

children.title: Chain-Transitive Limits
children.top_down_role: Limit sets characterized through approximate dynamical reachability.

knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Transitive Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Internal chain transitivity for compact invariant limit sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi\) be a continuous semiflow on a metric space \((X,d)\), and let \(L\subset X\) be nonempty and compact. For \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(T>0\), an \((\varepsilon,T)\)-chain in \(L\) from \(x\) to \(y\) consists of points \(x=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_m=y\) in \(L\) and times \(t_i\ge T\) such that
\[d(\Phi_{t_i}(x_i),x_{i+1})<\varepsilon\quad\text{for }i=0,\ldots,m-1.\]
The set \(L\) is internally chain transitive if such a chain exists for every \(x,y\in L\) and every \(\varepsilon,T>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact set is internally chain transitive when any two of its points can be connected inside it by arbitrarily accurate pseudo-orbit segments of arbitrarily long minimum duration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\) is internally chain transitive exactly when the displayed chain condition holds for all \(x,y\in L\) and all \(\varepsilon,T>0\).

notation.meaning: jump tolerance and minimum flow-segment duration
compact set within which every chain remains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chain condition is standard for a semiflow and the definition role fits the leaf, but the scope calls for compact invariant limit sets while invariance is absent from the defining assumptions. A source is also needed to determine whether the intended container includes the relation-based differential-inclusion variant.

children.title: Nonattracting Limit Behavior
children.top_down_role: Invariant limiting behavior lacking local attraction.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattracting Limit Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a compact invariant limit set that can occur without attracting any full neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Phi_t:X\to X be a continuous semiflow on a metric space \(X,d)\, and let \(L\subset X\ be nonempty, compact, and invariant. Its basin is \[\mathcal B(L)=\{x\in X:\operatorname{dist}(\Phi_t(x),L)\to0\text{ as }t\to\infty\}.\] The set \(L\ has nonattracting limit behavior when it is the \(\omega\-limit set of at least one trajectory but no open neighborhood of \(L\ is contained in \(\mathcal B(L)\. Thus convergence to \(L\ may occur from exceptional initial conditions without local attraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonattracting invariant set can be a trajectory’s limit set, yet every neighborhood contains initial states whose trajectories do not approach it.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ is a metric space and \(\Phi\ is a continuous semiflow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=\omega(x)\ for some \(x\in X\, while \(L\ has no neighborhood contained in \(\mathcal B(L)\.

notation.meaning: omega-limit set of the trajectory starting from x

review_flags: No supplied locator covers dynamical limit-set taxonomy.
Exact terminology varies between dynamical-systems references.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition fits the terminal container, but no source or inspectable locator establishes the intended meaning of “nonattracting limit behavior,” and that terminology is not sufficiently standardized to certify this formulation. The statement also contains numerous TeX commands outside complete math delimiters.

children.title: Lock-In Probability
children.top_down_role: Likelihood of remaining near a selected attracting region.

knowledge_statements.title: Lock-In Probability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional probability that stochastic approximation remains in an attracting basin and converges to its attractor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an adapted stochastic-approximation sequence \((x_n)\, an attractor \(A\ of the limiting flow, and an open set \(U\ with \(\overline U\subset\mathcal B(A)\, define the lock-in probability at time \(n\ by \[p_n(U,A)=\mathbb P\!\left(x_k\in\mathcal B(A)\text{ for every }k\ge n,\ \operatorname{dist}(x_k,A)\to0\mid\mathcal F_n,\ x_n\in U\right),\] whenever the conditioning event has positive probability. It quantifies basin retention and convergence after the iterate has entered a prescribed interior neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lock-in probability is the conditional chance that, after entering an interior basin neighborhood, all later iterates remain in the basin and converge to its attractor.
assumptions_latex: \(A\ is an attractor and \(\overline U\subset\mathcal B(A)\.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_n(U,A)\in[0,1]\ is the conditional probability of eventual retention in \(\mathcal B(A)\ and convergence to \(A\.

notation.meaning: lock-in probability from U at time n

review_flags: No stochastic-approximation lock-in theorem locator was supplied.
Definition should be aligned with the project’s preferred retention event.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The topic and definition role fit the container, but the conditioning notation combines conditioning on the sigma-field and on the event \(x_n\in U\) without a precise regular-conditional-probability convention. Stochastic-approximation references also use several distinct lock-in events. A source is needed to determine the intended event and hypotheses, and the statement has pervasive delimiter errors.

children.title: Attraction-Basin Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure governing deterministic attraction toward competing limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Attraction-Basin Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basin, boundary, and forward-invariance geometry for an attractor of the limiting flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi_t\ be a continuous semiflow on a metric space \(X\ and let \(A\subset X\ be compact and invariant. Its basin of attraction is \[\mathcal B(A)=\{x\in X:\operatorname{dist}(\Phi_t(x),A)\to0\text{ as }t\to\infty\}.\] If \(A\ is an attractor, then \(\mathcal B(A)\ is open and forward invariant: \(\Phi_t(\mathcal B(A))\subseteq\mathcal B(A)\ for every \(t\ge0\. Its boundary \(\partial\mathcal B(A)\ separates initial states selected by this attractor from states not converging to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attractor’s basin is the open, forward-invariant set of initial states converging to it; its boundary separates distinct asymptotic selections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B(A)\ is open and satisfies \(\Phi_t(\mathcal B(A))\subseteq\mathcal B(A)\ for all \(t\ge0\.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses attractors and basin geometry.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the geometry leaf, but openness of the stated convergence basin depends on the precise definition of attractor, which is not supplied. The claim that the boundary separates selections by distinct attractors is stronger than the formal assumptions, since points outside this basin need not converge to another attractor. A cited attractor definition is required, and the TeX delimiters are malformed.

children.title: Initialization Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of attractor selection on starting location.

knowledge_statements.title: Initialization Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates asymptotic attractor selection to the basin containing the initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\ be attractors of a limiting semiflow with pairwise disjoint basins \(\mathcal B_i\, and let \(x^\varepsilon\ be stochastic approximations whose perturbation level tends to zero. For every compact \(K\subset\mathcal B_i\ lying a positive distance from \(\partial\mathcal B_i\, basin consistency means \[\inf_{x_0^\varepsilon\in K}\mathbb P\!\left(\operatorname{dist}(x_n^\varepsilon,A_i)\to0\right)\longrightarrow1\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\downarrow0.\] Consequently, initializations in different basin interiors can select different limiting attractors, while initialization near a basin boundary need not have a stable selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under vanishing perturbations, initialization inside a basin selects its attractor with high probability; near basin boundaries, small initialization changes may alter the limit.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathcal B_i\ is compact with positive distance from the basin boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x_0^\varepsilon\in K}\mathbb P(\operatorname{dist}(x_n^\varepsilon,A_i)\to0)\to1\.
review_flags: The precise basin-consistency hypotheses depend on the stochastic-approximation model.
No matching source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the container, but basin membership and vanishing perturbation alone do not imply the displayed uniform convergence probability. The recursion, time horizon, noise scaling, stability or tracking assumptions, and meaning of convergence as \(n\to\infty\) must be specified by a source. The statement also contains unclosed math delimiters.

children.title: Noise-Driven Basin Escape
children.top_down_role: Departure from attraction basins under persistent stochastic fluctuations.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Driven Basin Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A constant-step stochastic recursion can escape every bounded deterministic attraction neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\alpha<1\ and let \((\xi_n)\ be independent standard Gaussian variables. The recursion \[x_{n+1}=(1-\alpha)x_n+\alpha\xi_{n+1}\] is a noisy discretization of the stable flow \(\dot x=-x\, whose attractor is \(\{0\}\. For every \(R>0\ and every initial value \(x_0\in[-R,R]\, \[\mathbb P\!\left(\sup_{n\ge0}|x_n|>R\right)=1.\] Hence nonvanishing unbounded noise prevents permanent lock-in to any bounded neighborhood, despite deterministic asymptotic stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With constant step size and Gaussian noise, a recursion around a stable equilibrium eventually exits every bounded neighborhood almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\sup_{n\ge0}|x_n|>R)=1\.

notation.meaning: radius of the proposed lock-in neighborhood

review_flags: Concrete claim is standard for an irreducible stationary Gaussian AR(1) chain, but no supporting locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind is appropriate and the Gaussian AR(1) escape claim is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source supports the almost-sure statement. Because this is a nontrivial recurrence claim rather than a definition, a specific locator is required. The statement also has pervasive delimiter errors.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Limits of Interpolated Trajectories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: ODE-method weak-limit theorem for time-shifted, piecewise-linear stochastic-approximation interpolations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(x_{n+1}=x_n+a_n(h(x_n)+M_{n+1}+r_n)\ in \(\mathbb R^d\, and form the piecewise-linear interpolation \(\bar x\ on times \(t_n=\sum_{k<n}a_k\. If \(h\ is locally Lipschitz, the iterates are almost surely bounded, \(a_n\downarrow0\ with \(\sum_n a_n=\infty\ and \(\sum_n a_n^2<\infty\, the martingale noise has uniformly bounded conditional second moments, and \(r_n\to0\, then every weak subsequential limit of \(\bar x(t_n+\cdot)\ is supported on solutions of \(\dot x=h(x)\.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard step-size, stability, and martingale-noise assumptions, every weak limit of shifted interpolated iterates follows the limiting ODE.
assumptions_latex: \(h\ is locally Lipschitz and \((x_n)\ is almost surely bounded.
\((M_{n+1})\ is martingale-difference noise with bounded conditional second moments, and \(r_n\to0\.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every weak subsequential limit of \(\bar x(t_n+\cdot)\ solves \(\dot x=h(x)\ almost surely.

notation.meaning: algorithmic time accumulated before iteration n

review_flags: No weak-convergence or stochastic-approximation source locator was supplied.
Function-space topology and filtration conditions require source alignment.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the weak-limit container, but “weak subsequential limit” is undefined without a path space and topology. The filtration, precise martingale-difference condition, uniform conditional-moment bound on bounded iterates, and mode of convergence of the remainder also require specification. No source locator is supplied, and the TeX delimiters are malformed.

children.title: Diffusion Approximations
children.top_down_role: Stochastic-process approximations near stable limiting behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Diffusion Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Ornstein–Uhlenbeck approximation for constant-step stochastic approximation near a stable equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{n+1}^{\eta}=x_n^{\eta}+\eta(h(x_n^{\eta})+\xi_{n+1})\, where \(h(x_\star)=0\ and \(H=Dh(x_\star)\ is Hurwitz. Suppose the conditional covariance of the martingale-difference noise converges locally to \(Q\ and a functional central-limit condition holds. For \(Z^{\eta}(t)=\eta^{-1/2}(x_{\lfloor t/\eta\rfloor}^{\eta}-x_\star)\, suitably interpolated and initialized with a weakly convergent scaled error, \[Z^{\eta}\Rightarrow Z,\qquad dZ_t=HZ_t\,dt+Q^{1/2}dW_t.\] The stationary covariance \(P\ of the limit satisfies \(HP+PH^{\mathsf T}+Q=0\.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After scaling fluctuations by the square root of the step size, constant-step iterates near a stable equilibrium converge weakly to an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck diffusion.
assumptions_latex: \(h\ is differentiable near \(x_\star\ and \(Dh(x_\star)\ is Hurwitz.
Noise is martingale-difference with local covariance limit \(Q\.
A functional central-limit and scaled-initialization condition holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z^{\eta}\Rightarrow Z\, where \(dZ_t=HZ_t\,dt+Q^{1/2}dW_t\.
review_flags: No diffusion-approximation source locator was supplied.
Precise tightness and functional central-limit hypotheses require certification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the diffusion-approximation leaf, but the functional central-limit condition, interpolation, path-space topology, localization near the equilibrium, and noise covariance assumptions are only named rather than stated. Those details determine whether the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck conclusion is valid. No supporting locator is supplied, and the statement has malformed delimiters.

knowledge_statements.title: Without-Replacement Mini-Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-population unbiasedness and variance correction for a uniformly sampled subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_N\in\mathbb R^d\ be a finite population with mean \(\bar g=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i\. If \(B\ is uniformly sampled from all subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\ having cardinality \(b\, define \(\widehat g_B=b^{-1}\sum_{i\in B}g_i\. Then \[\mathbb E[\widehat g_B]=\bar g,\qquad \mathbb E\|\widehat g_B-\bar g\|^2=\frac{N-b}{bN}\,S^2,\] where \(S^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\|g_i-\bar g\|^2\. Samples within the batch are dependent, and the finite-population correction makes the variance vanish when \(b=N\.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly sampled subset gives an unbiased finite-sum gradient, with variance reduced by the finite-population correction and zero variance for a full batch.
assumptions_latex: \(B\ is uniform over all subsets of size \(b\.
The vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_N\ are fixed conditional on the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_B]=\bar g\ and \(\mathbb E\|\widehat g_B-\bar g\|^2=(N-b)S^2/(bN)\.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Batch Sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Statistical consequence of holding the independent mini-batch size constant across iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose iteration \(k\ uses an average \(\bar G_k\ of a fixed number \(b\ge1\ of conditionally independent, unbiased stochastic gradients, each having conditional variance at most \(\sigma^2\. Then \[\mathbb E[\bar G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla F(x_k),\qquad \mathbb E[\|\bar G_k-\nabla F(x_k)\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le\frac{\sigma^2}{b}\] at every iteration. Thus a fixed finite batch reduces variance by a constant factor but does not force the estimator noise to vanish with \(k\; convergence requiring vanishing accumulated noise must instead be supplied by the step-size policy or stronger assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed batch gives a constant variance-reduction factor, but the stochastic gradient noise generally does not vanish as iterations proceed.
assumptions_latex: The batch size \(b\ is fixed and finite.
Samples within every batch are conditionally independent and unbiased.
Single-sample conditional variance is bounded by \(\sigma^2\.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The batch variance is at most \(\sigma^2/b\ uniformly in \(k\ and need not converge to zero.

The supplied locator is not confirmed to state this policy consequence, and the TeX delimiters are malformed.

children.title: Growing Batch Sizes

knowledge_statements.title: Growing Batch Sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded monotone batch policies in an infinite-sampling stochastic-gradient model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A growing batch-size policy is an integer sequence \(b_k\geq 1\) used in \(g_k=b_k^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b_k}G(x_k,\xi_{k,j})\) such that \(b_{k+1}\geq b_k\) for every \(k\) and \(b_k\to\infty\). The associated stochastic-gradient update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k g_k\). If the samples are conditionally independent and \(\mathbb E[G(x_k,\xi_{k,j})\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\), then \(g_k\) remains conditionally unbiased while its conditional covariance is divided by \(b_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A growing-batch SGD policy uses nondecreasing batch sizes tending to infinity, preserving unbiasedness while progressively reducing independent sampling noise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_k\to\infty\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(g_k\mid\mathcal F_k)=\operatorname{Cov}(G(x_k,\xi)\mid\mathcal F_k)/b_k\).

children.title: Adaptive Batch Sizes

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Batch Sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-dependent, nonanticipating batch selection for mini-batch SGD.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An adaptive batch-size policy selects an integer \(b_k\geq1\) that is measurable with respect to the pre-sampling history \(\mathcal F_k\), and then forms \(g_k=b_k^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b_k}G(x_k,\xi_{k,j})\). A variance-controlled instance chooses the smallest admissible \(b\) whose variance estimate \(\widehat V_k(b)\) satisfies \(\widehat V_k(b)/b\leq\theta^2\max\{\|\widehat g_k(b)\|^2,\varepsilon_k^2\}\), where \(\theta>0\) and \(\varepsilon_k>0\). The update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k\widehat g_k(b_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive policy chooses each batch from current history, often increasing it until estimated gradient noise is small relative to the estimated signal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_k=\min\{b\geq1:\widehat V_k(b)/b\leq\theta^2\max(\|\widehat g_k(b)\|^2,\varepsilon_k^2)\}\).

notation.meaning: estimated single-sample gradient variance at iteration k

children.title: Batch-Transition Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Batch-Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping-time transitions between prescribed mini-batch levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1\leq B_0<B_1<\cdots<B_m\) be prescribed batch levels and let \(0=\tau_0\leq\tau_1\leq\cdots\leq\tau_{m+1}=\infty\) be stopping times for the optimization filtration. A batch-transition regime is the policy \(b_k=B_r\) whenever \(\tau_r\leq k<\tau_{r+1}\). It is deterministic when every \(\tau_r\) is fixed in advance and adaptive when some \(\tau_r\) depends on observed iterates, gradients, or variance estimates. Nondecreasing levels ensure that every transition weakly increases sampling effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch-transition regime partitions iterations into phases, assigning a prescribed batch level to each phase and switching at deterministic or data-dependent stopping times.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_r\) is a stopping time for each \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_k=\sum_{r=0}^{m}B_r\mathbf 1_{\{\tau_r\leq k<\tau_{r+1}\}}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mini-Batch Variance Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conditional covariance scaling for independent, identically distributed samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(x_k\) measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_k\). Suppose \(G_{k,1},\ldots,G_{k,b}\) are conditionally independent and identically distributed with \(\mathbb E[G_{k,j}\mid\mathcal F_k]=
abla f(x_k)\) and conditional covariance \(\Sigma_k\). For \(g_k=b^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b}G_{k,j}\), one has \(\mathbb E[g_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=
abla f(x_k)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(g_k\mid\mathcal F_k)=\Sigma_k/b\). Consequently, \(\mathbb E[\|g_k-
abla f(x_k)\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_k)/b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging b conditionally independent unbiased gradients preserves unbiasedness and divides covariance and mean-square Euclidean error by b.
assumptions_latex: \(G_{k,1},\ldots,G_{k,b}\) are conditionally independent and identically distributed given \(\mathcal F_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Cov}(g_k\mid\mathcal F_k)=\Sigma_k/b\) and \(\mathbb E[\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_k)/b\).

children.title: Sample-Parallel Throughput
children.top_down_role: Worker utilization and throughput during parallel batch evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Parallel Throughput
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idealized synchronous throughput with balanced workers and logarithmic reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(p\) identical workers evaluate at most one sample gradient every \(c>0\) time units, a balanced batch of size \(b\) is partitioned across workers, and gradient reduction costs \(r\lceil\log_2 p\rceil\). Then one synchronous mini-batch requires at most \(T(b,p)=c\lceil b/p\rceil+r\lceil\log_2p\rceil\), giving throughput \(Q(b,p)=b/T(b,p)\). When communication is negligible and \(b\geq p\), \(Q(b,p)\) approaches \(p/c\); adding workers beyond \(b\) cannot reduce the evaluation term below \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced synchronous evaluation scales sample throughput nearly linearly up to the batch size, after which communication and insufficient samples limit further speedup.
assumptions_latex: Workers have equal evaluation cost and batches are balanced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(b,p)\leq c\lceil b/p\rceil+r\lceil\log_2p\rceil\) and \(Q(b,p)=b/T(b,p)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: ideal balanced-worker cost model with tree reduction
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is appropriate for this leaf, but the idealized hardware model has no citation. The phrase that a worker evaluates at most one sample every c time units describes a lower rate bound rather than the upper evaluation-time guarantee needed for the asserted upper bound on T(b,p).

children.title: Statistical–Computational Crossover
children.top_down_role: Batch-size ranges where added computation ceases to yield proportional statistical benefit.

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical–Computational Crossover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossover defined from a deterministic-plus-sampling-error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the error after \(K\) iterations with batch size \(b\) obeys \(E_K(b)\leq D_K+V_K/b\), where \(D_K>0\) is the batch-independent optimization term and \(V_K/b\) is the sampling term. The statistical crossover batch is \(b_{\mathrm{stat}}=\lceil V_K/D_K\rceil\). For \(b\geq b_{\mathrm{stat}}\), sampling contributes no more than the deterministic term, so \(E_K(b)\leq2D_K\); further batch growth can improve this bound by at most \(V_K/b\). With \(p\)-way sample parallelism, the useful linear-scaling range ends by \(b_{\mathrm{cross}}=\min\{p,b_{\mathrm{stat}}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The crossover occurs when mini-batch sampling error falls below batch-independent optimization error or when the batch exhausts available sample parallelism.
assumptions_latex: At most \(p\) samples can be evaluated concurrently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_{\mathrm{cross}}=\min\{p,\lceil V_K/D_K\rceil\}\), and \(b\geq b_{\mathrm{stat}}\) implies \(E_K(b)\leq2D_K\).

notation.meaning: batch-independent error term after K iterations

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: crossover derived from a canonical deterministic-plus-variance error decomposition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic statistical threshold follows from the assumed two-term upper bound, but the claim that the useful linear-scaling range ends at the minimum of p and that threshold depends on a particular runtime and convergence model. No source is supplied to support that interpretation or the selected bound model.

children.title: Parallel Batch Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Synchronous worker aggregation and straggler-sensitive minibatching.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Batch Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous worker averaging with explicit straggler-dependent completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(p\) workers, a batch partition \(S_k=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{p}S_{k,i}\), iterate \(x_k\), and step size \(\eta_k>0\), worker \(i\) computes \(s_{k,i}=\sum_{j\in S_{k,i}}G(x_k,\xi_j)\) and count \(n_{k,i}=|S_{k,i}|\). After every worker returns, the coordinator forms \(g_k=(\sum_i s_{k,i})/(\sum_i n_{k,i})\) and sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k g_k\). If worker times are \(T_{k,i}\) and reduction costs \(T_k^{\mathrm{red}}\), synchronous completion time is \(T_k=\max_iT_{k,i}+T_k^{\mathrm{red}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers compute disjoint gradient sums, a coordinator averages all returned samples, and each synchronous step waits for the slowest worker plus reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k\frac{\sum_i s_{k,i}}{\sum_i n_{k,i}}\) with \(T_k=\max_iT_{k,i}+T_k^{\mathrm{red}}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Stochastic Gradient Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\) be differentiable on a neighborhood of \(C\). knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Projection Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-iteration oracle cost of exact Euclidean projected stochastic methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\eta_kG_k)\). If producing \(G_k\) costs \(T_G(d)\), computing the exact Euclidean projection \(\Pi_C(y)=\arg\min_{x\in C}\|x-y\|_2^2/2\) costs \(T_{\Pi_C}(d)\), and vector arithmetic costs \(O(d)\), then one iteration costs \(T_G(d)+T_{\Pi_C}(d)+O(d)\) time and makes one stochastic-oracle call and one projection-oracle call. Thus \(K\) iterations cost \(K[T_G(d)+T_{\Pi_C}(d)+O(d)]\); projection dominates whenever \(T_{\Pi_C}(d)=\omega(T_G(d)+d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each projected stochastic step needs one gradient-oracle call and one projection; expensive feasible-set projections can dominate total runtime.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The projection is computed exactly by a projection oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_K=K[T_G(d)+T_{\Pi_C}(d)+O(d)]\), with projection dominance if \(T_{\Pi_C}(d)=\omega(T_G(d)+d)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Proximal Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean stochastic proximal-gradient iteration for a smooth expected loss plus a proper convex regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an initial point \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom} r\), at iteration \(t\geq 0\) obtain a random vector \(g_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\), choose \(\alpha_t>0\), and set
\[
x_{t+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha_t r}(x_t-\alpha_t g_t)
=\mathop{\arg\min}_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{r(x)+\frac{1}{2\alpha_t}\lVert x-(x_t-\alpha_tg_t)\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
After a prescribed number \(T\) of oracle calls, output either \(x_T\) or a specified weighted average of \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace the smooth gradient by an unbiased stochastic estimate, take a forward step, and apply the proximal map of the nonsmooth regularizer.

\((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\) is the history filtration and \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) is a stochastic forward step for \(f\) followed by a proximal step for \(r\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic resolvent splitting for a cocoercive single-valued operator and a maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_0\in\mathcal H\). At iteration \(t\geq0\), observe \(b_t\) with \(\mathbb E[b_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=B x_t\), choose \(\gamma_t>0\), and compute
\[
x_{t+1}=J_{\gamma_t A}(x_t-\gamma_t b_t),\qquad J_{\gamma_t A}=(I+\gamma_t A)^{-1}.
\]
Equivalently, the update satisfies \(0\in A x_{t+1}+b_t+\gamma_t^{-1}(x_{t+1}-x_t)\). A finite run returns \(x_T\), while asymptotic formulations study the entire adapted sequence \((x_t)_{t\geq0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate the forward operator stochastically, take an explicit step, and apply the resolvent of the maximally monotone backward operator.

\(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and \(\mathbb E[\lVert b_t\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_t]<\infty\).
The target problem is to find \(x_\star\) satisfying \(0\in A x_\star+B x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) is obtained by a stochastic forward evaluation of \(B\) and an implicit backward evaluation of \(A\).

children.title: Heavy-Ball Stochastic Gradient Methods
children.top_down_role: Classical velocity-based momentum under stochastic noise.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Ball Stochastic Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical stochastic heavy-ball recursion with a velocity state and current-point gradient sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), initialize \(v_0=0\). For \(t\geq0\), sample \(g_t\) with \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\), choose \(\alpha_t>0\) and momentum \(\beta_t\in[0,1)\), and update
\[
v_{t+1}=\beta_t v_t+g_t,\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_t v_{t+1}.
\]
Equivalently, when \(\alpha_t=\alpha_{t-1}\), \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tg_t+\beta_t(x_t-x_{t-1})\). After \(T\) iterations, output \(x_T\) or a declared average of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-ball SGD exponentially carries past stochastic gradients in a velocity and steps opposite the resulting momentum direction.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t,v_t\) are \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and \(g_t\) has finite conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_t,v_t)\) obeys a stochastic first-order recursion with geometrically weighted gradient memory.

notation.meaning: Stochastic gradient sampled at the current iterate.

review_flags: authoritative stochastic heavy-ball source and exact normalization locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursion is mathematically coherent and fits the heavy-ball stochastic-gradient container, including the stated constant-stepsize equivalence. Because stochastic heavy-ball conventions differ in velocity normalization, an authoritative source with an exact algorithm or equation locator is required.

children.title: Nesterov-Type Stochastic Momentum
children.top_down_role: Look-ahead and accelerated-style stochastic momentum families.

knowledge_statements.title: Nesterov-Type Stochastic Momentum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Look-ahead stochastic momentum using a gradient sampled at an extrapolated point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_{-1}=x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), for \(t\geq0\) choose \(\beta_t\in[0,1)\) and \(\alpha_t>0\), form
\[
y_t=x_t+\beta_t(x_t-x_{t-1}),
\]
sample \(g_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla f(y_t)\), and update
\[
x_{t+1}=y_t-\alpha_t g_t.
\]
The method returns \(x_T\), \(y_T\), or a prespecified weighted average after \(T\) stochastic-gradient calls; the choice must be declared by the particular convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extrapolate from the two latest iterates, evaluate a stochastic gradient at that look-ahead point, and step from the extrapolated point.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t,x_{t-1}\) are \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and \(g_t\) has finite conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) combines inertial extrapolation with a stochastic gradient evaluated at the extrapolated state \(y_t\).

notation.meaning: Stochastic gradient evaluated at the look-ahead point.

review_flags: Nesterov-type stochastic momentum has multiple inequivalent recursions; exact local variant needs an authoritative source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The look-ahead recursion is a plausible Nesterov-type stochastic momentum algorithm and fits the container, but several inequivalent stochastic Nesterov recursions exist. A source identifying this exact extrapolate-sample-update variant is required.

children.title: Gradient-Velocity Averaging Coupling
children.top_down_role: Averaging mechanisms used as momentum states or noise filters.

children.title: Gradient Averaging States
children.top_down_role: Averaged gradient information used for stochastic noise filtering.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Averaging States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive weighted averaging state for stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((g_t)_{t\geq1}\subset\mathbb R^d\) be stochastic gradient observations and let \(a_t\in(0,1]\). A gradient averaging state is the adapted sequence \((m_t)_{t\geq0}\) defined by \(m_0=0\) and
\[
m_t=(1-a_t)m_{t-1}+a_tg_t.
\]
Consequently,
\[
m_t=\sum_{s=1}^{t}a_s\!\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{t}(1-a_j)\right)g_s.
\]
For constant \(a_t=a\), the weight assigned to \(g_s\) at time \(t\) is \(a(1-a)^{t-s}\), so the state is an exponentially weighted, generally unnormalized average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient averaging state recursively combines the previous state with the newest stochastic gradient, yielding explicit geometrically decaying weights when the coefficient is constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_t\) is a causal weighted sum of \(g_1,\ldots,g_t\).

notation.meaning: Weight assigned to the new gradient observation.

review_flags: local intended averaging convention and supporting source are unspecified

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursive expansion is correct and definition is an appropriate content kind for this state container. No evidence establishes that this particular normalized exponential-average convention is the intended local meaning of Gradient Averaging States.

children.title: Velocity Averaging States
children.top_down_role: Smoothed inertial states used to control stochastic motion.

knowledge_statements.title: Velocity Averaging States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive averaging of displacement or velocity observations in an inertial stochastic method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((u_t)_{t\geq1}\subset\mathbb R^d\) be velocity observations, such as \(u_t=x_t-x_{t-1}\), and let \(b_t\in(0,1]\). A velocity averaging state is the adapted sequence \((v_t)_{t\geq0}\) defined by \(v_0=0\) and
\[
v_t=(1-b_t)v_{t-1}+b_tu_t.
\]
Thus
\[
v_t=\sum_{s=1}^{t}b_s\!\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{t}(1-b_j)\right)u_s.
\]
When \(b_t=b\), past velocities receive geometrically decreasing weights \(b(1-b)^{t-s}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A velocity averaging state filters observed displacements or velocities through a causal weighted recursion, with geometric memory under a constant averaging coefficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_t\) is a causal weighted sum of the velocity observations \(u_1,\ldots,u_t\).

notation.meaning: Observed instantaneous velocity or iterate displacement.
Weight assigned to the newest velocity observation.

review_flags: velocity averaging may instead denote momentum itself in the intended source; exact convention requires evidence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursion and its weighted-sum expansion are correct, and definition fits the terminal container. Evidence is needed because velocity averaging may denote an averaged displacement, a momentum state, or another inertial state under different conventions.

children.title: Coupled Averaging Effects
children.top_down_role: Stability and responsiveness consequences of combining averaged state mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Averaging Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-state linear filtering effect when gradient and velocity averages are updated together.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(m_t=(1-a)m_{t-1}+ag_t\) and \(v_t=(1-b)v_{t-1}+bu_t\), where \(a,b\in(0,1]\) and \(m_0=v_0=0\). Then
\[
(m_t,v_t)=\sum_{s=1}^{t}\bigl(a(1-a)^{t-s}g_s,\;b(1-b)^{t-s}u_s\bigr).
\]
Hence the two states have distinct geometric memory lengths controlled by \(a\) and \(b\). If an iterate update uses \(d_t=m_t+\lambda v_t\), then \(d_t\) is the sum of two causal filters and cannot generally be represented by one geometric filter unless their decay factors coincide or the input sequences satisfy an additional relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupling gradient and velocity averages combines two filters with potentially different memory scales; generally their summed direction is not a single exponential average.
assumptions_latex: Both averaging states start from zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled direction \(d_t=m_t+\lambda v_t\) contains two independently weighted histories, except in degenerate or specially related cases.

notation.meaning: Direction formed by coupling the two states.

review_flags: the algebraic property is precise, but the taxonomy's intended coupled averaging model lacks a source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed two-filter identity is algebraically correct, and property is the right mathematical role. The taxonomy's intended coupled averaging mechanism is not evidenced, so the claimed model and its interpretation cannot yet be tied reliably to this leaf.

children.title: Data-Adaptive Preconditioning Family
children.top_down_role: Data-dependent scaling and stabilization mechanisms for stochastic gradients.

children.title: AdaGrad-Type Accumulated-Geometry Methods
children.top_down_role: Scalar, diagonal, and matrix accumulated-gradient scaling families.

knowledge_statements.title: AdaGrad-Type Accumulated-Geometry Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal AdaGrad with cumulative coordinatewise squared-gradient geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_1\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), \(s_0=0\), \(\delta>0\), and \(\eta>0\), for \(t=1,\ldots,T\) obtain a stochastic subgradient \(g_t\), set
\[
s_t=s_{t-1}+g_t\odot g_t,\qquad H_t=\operatorname{Diag}\!\bigl(\sqrt{s_t}+\delta\mathbf 1\bigr),
\]
and update
\[
x_{t+1}=\mathop{\arg\min}_{x\in X}\left\{\eta\langle g_t,x\rangle+\tfrac12\lVert x-x_t\rVert_{H_t}^{2}\right\}.
\]
After \(T\) oracle calls, output \(x_{T+1}\) or a prespecified average. Scalar and full-matrix variants replace \(H_t\) by their corresponding accumulated geometries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AdaGrad accumulates squared gradients and uses their square roots as an adaptive metric, reducing steps in coordinates with large historical gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(g_t\) is an observed stochastic subgradient at \(x_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is a projected stochastic first-order step in the cumulative gradient-dependent metric \(H_t\).

notation.meaning: Quadratic form z transpose H_t z.

children.title: RMSProp-Type Moving-Moment Scaling
children.top_down_role: Second-moment moving-average scaling in RMSProp-type methods.

knowledge_statements.title: RMSProp-Type Moving-Moment Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise RMSProp recursion using an exponential average of squared stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), initialize \(v_0=0\). For \(t\geq1\), sample a stochastic gradient \(g_t\) at \(x_{t-1}\), choose \(\rho\in[0,1)\), \(\alpha_t>0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), and compute
\[
v_t=\rho v_{t-1}+(1-\rho)(g_t\odot g_t),\qquad
x_t=x_{t-1}-\alpha_t\,g_t\oslash(\sqrt{v_t}+\varepsilon\mathbf1).
\]
All square roots and divisions are coordinatewise. After \(T\) stochastic-gradient calls, return \(x_T\) or another output explicitly prescribed by the application.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RMSProp divides each stochastic-gradient coordinate by a stabilized moving root-mean-square estimate of that coordinate's recent gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(g_t\in\mathbb R^d\) is a stochastic gradient observed at \(x_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each coordinate is scaled by the reciprocal of its exponentially averaged recent root-mean-square gradient magnitude.

notation.meaning: Exponential moving average of coordinatewise squared gradients.

review_flags: authoritative RMSProp source and exact epsilon placement locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated recursion is a standard RMSProp-type algorithm and fits the terminal container. An authoritative locator is required because published and implementation variants differ in decay parameterization and whether epsilon is placed inside or outside the square root.

children.title: Adam-Type Moving-Moment Scaling
children.top_down_role: Coupled first-moment and second-moment scaling in Adam-type methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Adam-Type Moving-Moment Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adam recursion with bias-corrected first and second exponential gradient moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), set \(m_0=v_0=0\). For \(t\geq1\), sample \(g_t\) at \(x_{t-1}\) and compute
\[
m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\qquad
v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)(g_t\odot g_t),
\]
\[
\widehat m_t=\frac{m_t}{1-\beta_1^t},\qquad
\widehat v_t=\frac{v_t}{1-\beta_2^t},\qquad
x_t=x_{t-1}-\alpha_t\widehat m_t\oslash(\sqrt{\widehat v_t}+\varepsilon\mathbf1).
\]
After \(T\) stochastic-gradient calls, output \(x_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adam combines bias-corrected moving averages of gradients and squared gradients, scaling the former by the stabilized square root of the latter.
assumptions_latex: \(g_t\in\mathbb R^d\) is a stochastic gradient at \(x_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update uses a coordinatewise normalized, bias-corrected first-moment direction.

children.title: Moving-Moment Bias Correction
children.top_down_role: Finite-horizon corrections for initialized exponential moment estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Moving-Moment Bias Correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact zero-initialization correction for exponential moving moments under a stationary conditional mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_1,z_2,\ldots\) be integrable random vectors with \(\mathbb E[z_t]=\mu\), and let \(q_0=0\) and \(q_t=\beta q_{t-1}+(1-\beta)z_t\) for a constant \(\beta\in[0,1)\). Then
\[
q_t=(1-\beta)\sum_{s=1}^{t}\beta^{t-s}z_s,
\qquad
\mathbb E[q_t]=(1-\beta^t)\mu.
\]
Therefore the corrected state \(\widehat q_t=q_t/(1-\beta^t)\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[\widehat q_t]=\mu\). Applied separately to gradient and squared-gradient observations, this yields the standard Adam corrections \(m_t/(1-\beta_1^t)\) and \(v_t/(1-\beta_2^t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-initialized exponential average is shrunk by one minus beta to the power t; dividing by that factor removes this initialization bias under stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(z_t\) is integrable and has the same mean \(\mu\) for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat q_t=q_t/(1-\beta^t)\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\mu\).

children.title: Convergence-Sensitive Denominator Variants
children.top_down_role: Denominator constructions that alter stability or convergence behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence-Sensitive Denominator Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: AMSGrad-style monotone second-moment denominator designed to prevent increases in effective coordinatewise steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x_0\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and \(m_0=v_0=\widehat v_0=0\). For \(t\geq1\), observe \(g_t\), choose \(\beta_{1,t}\in[0,1)\), \(\beta_2\in[0,1)\), and \(\alpha_t>0\), and set
\[
m_t=\beta_{1,t}m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{1,t})g_t,
\]
\[
v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)(g_t\odot g_t),\qquad
\widehat v_t=\max\{\widehat v_{t-1},v_t\},
\]
where the maximum is coordinatewise. Update \(x_t\) by projecting \(x_{t-1}-\alpha_tm_t\oslash(\sqrt{\widehat v_t}+\varepsilon\mathbf1)\) onto \(X\), and output \(x_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AMSGrad replaces Adam's current second moment by its coordinatewise running maximum, preventing the adaptive denominator from decreasing.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(g_t\) is a stochastic gradient available at iteration \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat v_t\geq\widehat v_{t-1}\) coordinatewise, so the unregularized coordinatewise denominator is nondecreasing.

notation.meaning: Coordinatewise running maximum of second-moment states.

children.title: Gradient Magnitude-Control Family

children.title: Normalized Stochastic Gradients
children.top_down_role: Direction-preserving magnitude normalization for stochastic gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Stochastic Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SGD whose oracle direction is rescaled to unit norm, with a zero-gradient convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an initial point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), stepsizes \(\eta_k>0\), and stochastic gradient samples \(g_k=G(x_k,\xi_k)\), define \(d_k=0\) when \(g_k=0\) and \(d_k=g_k/\lVert g_k\rVert_2\) otherwise. The normalized stochastic-gradient iteration is
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k d_k.
\]
After a prescribed number \(K\) of oracle calls, output either the final iterate \(x_K\) or a stated average or randomized iterate. Normalization fixes every nonzero update length at \(\eta_k\); it does not generally preserve unbiasedness even when \(\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide each nonzero sampled gradient by its Euclidean norm before stepping. This bounds the update length but generally turns an unbiased gradient sample into a biased direction.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta_k>0\) and the output convention are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k g_k/\lVert g_k\rVert_2\) for \(g_k\ne0\), with \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) for \(g_k=0\).

children.title: Clipped Stochastic Gradients
children.top_down_role: Magnitude truncation for stability under large stochastic gradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Clipped Stochastic Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean norm clipping at a fixed or predictable positive threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), stepsizes \(\eta_k>0\), thresholds \(\tau_k>0\), and samples \(g_k=G(x_k,\xi_k)\), set
\[
\widetilde g_k=\operatorname{clip}_{\tau_k}(g_k):=g_k\min\left\{1,\frac{\tau_k}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2}\right\},
\]
where the multiplier is defined as \(1\) when \(g_k=0\). Update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k\widetilde g_k\) and return the prescribed final, averaged, or randomized iterate after \(K\) calls. Then \(\lVert\widetilde g_k\rVert_2\le\tau_k\), while conditional unbiasedness need not survive clipping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clip each sampled gradient to a threshold before applying the SGD step. The resulting direction has bounded norm, but clipping generally introduces conditional bias.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_k>0\) is fixed in advance or measurable before observing \(g_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k\operatorname{clip}_{\tau_k}(g_k)\) and \(\lVert\operatorname{clip}_{\tau_k}(g_k)\rVert_2\le\tau_k\).
