children.title: Magnitude-Threshold Regimes
children.top_down_role: Threshold choices across noise, curvature, and scale regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Magnitude-Threshold Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise representation of Euclidean clipping below, at, and above its threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(g\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\tau>0\), Euclidean clipping admits the regime decomposition
\[
\operatorname{clip}_{\tau}(g)=
\begin{cases}
g, & \lVert g\rVert_2\le\tau,\\
\tau g/\lVert g\rVert_2, & \lVert g\rVert_2>\tau.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus the small-magnitude regime leaves the stochastic gradient unchanged, the boundary \(\lVert g\rVert_2=\tau\) joins the formulas continuously, and the large-magnitude regime retains only the direction and caps the norm at \(\tau\). Equivalently, \(\lVert\operatorname{clip}_{\tau}(g)\rVert_2=\min\{\lVert g\rVert_2,\tau\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Below the threshold, clipping changes nothing; above it, clipping preserves direction and replaces the norm by the threshold. The two formulas agree at the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert\operatorname{clip}_{\tau}(g)\rVert_2=\min\{\lVert g\rVert_2,\tau\}\).
review_flags: exact representation is standard but no clipping-specific locator was supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The piecewise representation is mathematically correct and fits the leaf, but no source with an inspectable clipping-specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Robustness–Bias Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Bias and stability consequences of aggressive magnitude control.

knowledge_statements.title: Robustness–Bias Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional bias and second-moment control induced by norm clipping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g\) be an integrable stochastic gradient with \(\mathbb{E}[g\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\), and let \(\widetilde g=\operatorname{clip}_{\tau}(g)\) for \(\tau>0\). Then
\[
\lVert\widetilde g\rVert_2\le\tau,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\lVert\widetilde g\rVert_2^2\mid x]\le\tau^2,
\]
but its conditional bias is
\[
\mathbb{E}[\widetilde g\mid x]-\nabla f(x)
=-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(1-\frac{\tau}{\lVert g\rVert_2}\right)g\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\lVert g\rVert_2>\tau\}}\middle|x\right].
\]
Hence clipping limits the influence and second moment of large samples while generally introducing bias supported on the clipped tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clipping uniformly bounds sample influence and second moments, but its expected direction is generally biased. The bias comes exactly from samples whose norms exceed the threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is conditionally integrable and \(\mathbb{E}[g\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert\widetilde g\rVert_2^2\mid x]\le\tau^2\), with the displayed tail-supported conditional bias.
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports the clipping bias identity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm, second-moment, and tail-supported bias identities are correct under the stated assumptions, but the nontrivial bias formula lacks a cited source and locator.

children.title: Variance-Reduction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interfaces from plain SGD to estimator-memory methods treated fully in the finite-sum optimization chapter.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Reduction Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between memoryless unbiased SGD oracles and finite-sum estimators with persistent control-variate state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite sum \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), plain SGD samples \(i_k\) and uses \(g_k=\nabla f_{i_k}(x_k)\), so \(\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\) but its conditional variance need not vanish at a minimizer. A method crosses the variance-reduction boundary when its estimator additionally uses persistent state—such as a reference full gradient or stored component gradients—to form \(v_k\) satisfying a decreasing or vanishing variance bound. Such estimator-memory constructions are not instances of memoryless plain SGD, even when the primal update remains \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_kv_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Plain SGD uses a fresh component gradient whose variance may persist at an optimum. Reference gradients or stored component gradients cross into finite-sum variance-reduction methods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Persistent estimator state that controls or eliminates component-sampling variance marks departure from memoryless plain SGD.
review_flags: boundary wording requires chapter-level source alignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits a failure-boundary container and appropriately distinguishes memoryless component sampling from persistent estimator-memory constructions, but this chapter boundary and the variance behavior need a finite-sum variance-reduction source.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex Stochastic Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected objective error for projected stochastic subgradient descent with constant stepsize and averaged output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex with minimizer \(x^*\), and suppose \(g_k\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid x_k]\in\partial f(x_k)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2\mid x_k]\le G^2\). For \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_X(x_k-\eta g_k)\), \(\eta>0\), and \(\bar x_K=K^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}x_k\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[f(\bar x_K)-f(x^*)]\le \frac{\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2}{2\eta K}+\frac{\eta G^2}{2}.
\]
Choosing \(\eta=\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2/(G\sqrt K)\) gives error at most \(G\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2/\sqrt K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaged projected stochastic subgradient descent achieves expected objective error proportional to one over the square root of the number of oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f\) is convex with a minimizer \(x^*\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[f(\bar x_K)-f(x^*)]\le \lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2/(2\eta K)+\eta G^2/2\).

notation.meaning: arithmetic average of the first \(K\) iterates

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex SGD
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected objective error for averaged SGD under convex smoothness and bounded stochastic-gradient variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and \(L\)-smooth with minimizer \(x^*\). Suppose \(g_k\) is conditionally unbiased and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\rVert_2^2\mid x_k]\le\sigma^2\). For \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta g_k\), a constant \(0<\eta\le 1/L\), and \(\bar x_K=K^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}x_k\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[f(\bar x_K)-f(x^*)]\le \frac{\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2}{2\eta K}+\frac{\eta\sigma^2}{2}.
\]
Thus a suitable horizon-dependent \(\eta\) yields the standard deterministic-transient plus \(O(\sigma/\sqrt K)\) stochastic term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth convex objectives, averaged SGD has a deterministic transient inversely proportional to stepsize times iterations and a noise term proportional to stepsize.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[f(\bar x_K)-f(x^*)]\le \lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2/(2\eta K)+\eta\sigma^2/2\).

children.title: Strongly Convex SGD
children.top_down_role: Curvature-supported stochastic rate and averaging regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex SGD
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-square SGD recursion and noise floor under strong convexity and smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth with minimizer \(x^*\). Suppose \(g_k\) is conditionally unbiased and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\rVert_2^2\mid x_k]\le\sigma^2\). For constant-step SGD \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta g_k\) with \(0<\eta\le1/L\),
\[
\mathbb{E}\lVert x_K-x^*\rVert_2^2
\le (1-\mu\eta)^K\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2+\frac{\eta\sigma^2}{\mu}.
\]
Consequently, constant stepsizes converge geometrically to a noise neighborhood; decreasing stepsizes or suitable averaging are required for vanishing stochastic error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity gives geometric mean-square contraction under a constant stepsize, but persistent gradient noise leaves a neighborhood whose size is proportional to the stepsize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\lVert x_K-x^*\rVert_2^2\le(1-\mu\eta)^K\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2+\eta\sigma^2/\mu\).

children.title: Polyak–Łojasiewicz Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stochastic convergence regimes governed by gradient domination.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyak–Łojasiewicz Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global or region-restricted Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient-dominance condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A differentiable function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) with attained minimum value \(f^*\) satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition with parameter \(\mu>0\) on a set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) if
\[
\frac12\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\ge\mu\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)
\quad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
The condition is global when \(D=\mathbb{R}^d\) and local when \(D\) is a proper validity region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PL condition lower-bounds squared gradient norm by objective suboptimality on a specified region. It is global when that region is the whole space and local otherwise.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and attains its minimum value \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac12\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\ge\mu(f(x)-f^*)\) for every \(x\in D\).

notation.meaning: region on which the PL inequality holds

children.title: Error-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stochastic convergence regimes governed by residual-to-solution growth control.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient error bound controlling distance to the minimizer set on a specified region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f\), and let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). A gradient error bound with constant \(\kappa>0\) holds on \(D\) when
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2
\quad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
The regime is global if \(D=\mathbb{R}^d\), and local if \(D\) is a neighborhood or sublevel set containing \(X^*\). For stochastic methods the inequality constrains the true gradient; transferring it to sampled gradients requires separate noise assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient error bound says distance to the solution set is controlled by the true gradient norm. It may hold globally or only near the solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2\) for every \(x\in D\).

children.title: Geometry Implication Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Implication and separation relationships among domination, growth, and error-bound conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry Implication Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth global PL function need not be convex, establishing a boundary on geometry implications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(g(x)=x+\tfrac12\sin x\) and \(f(x)=g(x)^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Since \(g'(x)=1+\tfrac12\cos x\ge\tfrac12\), \(g\) is strictly increasing, has the unique zero \(0\), and \(f^*=0\). Moreover,
\[
\frac12|f'(x)|^2=2g(x)^2g'(x)^2\ge\frac12 f(x),
\]
so \(f\) satisfies the global PL inequality with \(\mu=\tfrac12\). However,
\[
f''(x)=2g'(x)^2-g(x)\sin x
\]
is negative at \(x=\tfrac\pi2+2\pi m\) for all sufficiently large integers \(m\). Thus global PL geometry alone implies neither convexity nor strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A squared monotone nonlinear residual satisfies a global PL inequality yet is nonconvex. Therefore PL geometry alone does not imply convexity or strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) satisfies global PL with \(\mu=1/2\) but is not convex.
review_flags: self-contained counterexample lacks an external source locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally correct and establishes that global PL does not imply convexity or strong convexity, but the nontrivial example has no external source locator.

children.title: Local Geometry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Guarantees available only within neighborhoods exhibiting favorable growth geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Geometry Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PL or gradient error-bound geometry restricted to a neighborhood or invariant sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with attained minimum value \(f^*\), nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\), and region \(D\supseteq X^*\). A local PL regime holds on \(D\) if there exists \(\mu>0\) such that
\[
\frac12\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\ge\mu\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)
\quad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
A local gradient error-bound regime holds on \(D\) if there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2
\quad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
A convergence guarantee using either local condition applies only while the iterates remain in \(D\); initialization in \(D\) alone does not ensure invariance under stochastic noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local PL and local gradient error-bound conditions are distinct inequalities that may hold on a restricted region. A stochastic convergence argument using either condition must ensure that its iterates remain in that region.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable, attains \(f^*\), and has nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any guarantee based on a displayed local inequality requires \(x_k\in D\) throughout the analyzed horizon.
review_flags: no supplied locator supports the local geometry conditions or stochastic-invariance boundary

children.title: Composite Nonconvex Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Proximal and generalized-gradient stationarity regimes for composite objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Nonconvex Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient stationarity for a smooth nonconvex term plus a proper closed convex term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+h\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(f\) is differentiable and \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex. For \(\eta>0\), define the proximal-gradient mapping by \[G_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}\!\left(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\right).\] A point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\) is stationary exactly when \(G_\eta(x)=0\), equivalently \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\). A random output \(X\) is expected \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when \(\mathbb{E}\|G_\eta(X)\|^2\leq\varepsilon^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite stationarity is measured by the proximal-gradient mapping; its zeros satisfy the generalized first-order condition, and its expected squared norm defines stochastic approximate stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_\eta(x)=0\iff 0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\), with approximate stationarity measured by \(\mathbb{E}\|G_\eta(X)\|^2\).

notation.meaning: Proximal mapping of the scaled function eta h.
Proximal-gradient mapping at step size eta.

children.title: Expected-Value Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Guarantees through expected objective, distance, or stationarity measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Value Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation-mode guarantees for nonnegative stochastic error criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_T\) be the output of a stochastic optimization method after budget \(T\), and let \(M:\mathcal{X}\to[0,+\infty]\) be a measurable error criterion, such as objective gap, squared distance to a solution set, or squared stationarity residual. An expected-value guarantee at budget \(T\) is an inequality \[\mathbb{E}[M(X_T)]\leq B(T),\] where the expectation covers all algorithmic and oracle randomness. The method attains expected accuracy \(\varepsilon\) when \(B(T)\leq\varepsilon\); for squared residual conventions, the target may instead be written \(B(T)\leq\varepsilon^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expected-value guarantee bounds the mean of a specified measurable optimization error after a stated budget, with the accuracy convention declared explicitly.
assumptions_latex: \(X_T\) is a random element of a measurable space \(\mathcal{X}\).
\(M\) is measurable, nonnegative, and integrable at \(X_T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[M(X_T)]\leq B(T)\), with expected accuracy achieved whenever the declared threshold holds.

notation.meaning: Declared objective, distance, or stationarity error criterion.
Deterministic upper bound as a function of budget.

children.title: High-Probability Guarantees

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Confidence-parameterized tail guarantees for a declared stochastic optimization error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_T\) be the output after budget \(T\), and let \(M:\mathcal{X}\to[0,+\infty]\) be measurable. A high-probability guarantee is a family of bounds indexed by \(\delta\in(0,1)\) such that \[\mathbb{P}\!\left(M(X_T)\leq B(T,\delta)\right)\geq 1-\delta.\] Equivalently, \(\mathbb{P}(M(X_T)>B(T,\delta))\leq\delta\). A claimed \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-guarantee must specify a budget \(T(\varepsilon,\delta)\) satisfying \(B(T(\varepsilon,\delta),\delta)\leq\varepsilon\), together with the randomness and tail assumptions covered by the probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-probability guarantee bounds a declared error with failure probability at most delta and states how the required budget depends on accuracy and confidence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(M(X_T)>B(T,\delta))\leq\delta\).

children.title: Almost-Sure Convergence
children.top_down_role: Pathwise convergence under diminishing gains, stability, and controlled stochastic errors.

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robbins–Siegmund-type pathwise convergence criterion used in stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal{F}_k)\) be a filtration and let \(V_k,U_k,A_k,B_k\) be nonnegative, \(\mathcal{F}_k\)-measurable random variables satisfying \[\mathbb{E}[V_{k+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\leq(1+A_k)V_k-U_k+B_k\quad\text{almost surely}.\] If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}A_k<\infty\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B_k<\infty\) almost surely, then \(V_k\) converges almost surely to a finite random variable and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}U_k<\infty\) almost surely. When \(U_k\) dominates a stationarity or distance residual, this yields its corresponding pathwise summability conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative stochastic Lyapunov sequence converges almost surely when its conditional drift has summable multiplicative and additive errors, and its descent terms are summable.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional drift inequality holds almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_k\) converges to a finite limit almost surely and \(\sum_k U_k<\infty\) almost surely.

children.title: Convergence in Probability

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence in Probability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence in probability for random optimization iterates or residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_n\) and \(X\) be random elements defined on a common probability space and taking values in a metric space \((S,d)\). The sequence \((X_n)\) converges in probability to \(X\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}X\), if for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\!\left(d(X_n,X)>\varepsilon\right)=0.\] For a nonnegative scalar optimization residual \(R_n\), convergence in probability to zero means \(\mathbb{P}(R_n>\varepsilon)\to0\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iterates converge in probability when the chance of remaining farther than any fixed tolerance from the limit tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X_n\) and \(X\) are random elements on one probability space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}X\iff \mathbb{P}(d(X_n,X)>\varepsilon)\to0\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).

children.title: Convergence in Distribution

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence in Distribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of random optimization outputs on a metric state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_n\) and \(X\) be random elements taking values in a metric space \(S\), with laws \(\mu_n\) and \(\mu\). The sequence \((X_n)\) converges in distribution to \(X\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\), if \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_n)]=\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X)]\] for every bounded continuous function \(\varphi:S\to\mathbb{R}\). Equivalently, the probability measures \(\mu_n\) converge weakly to \(\mu\). The variables need not be realized on a common probability space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outputs converge in distribution when expectations of every bounded continuous test function converge to those under the limiting law.
assumptions_latex: \(X_n\) and \(X\) take values in a metric space \(S\).
All test functions \(\varphi:S\to\mathbb{R}\) are bounded and continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\iff \int_S\varphi\,d\mu_n\to\int_S\varphi\,d\mu\) for every bounded continuous \(\varphi\).

notation.meaning: Probability laws of the random elements.

children.title: Probabilistic Implication Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Relationships and non-implications among probability-mode guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Implication Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict implication boundaries among almost-sure, probability, and distributional convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For random elements in a metric space, \[X_n\to X\ \text{almost surely}\ \Longrightarrow\ X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}X\ \Longrightarrow\ X_n\xrightarrow{d}X.\] Neither converse holds in general. If independent events \((A_n)\) satisfy \(\mathbb{P}(A_n)=1/n\) and \(X_n=\mathbf{1}_{A_n}\), then \(X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0\) but \(X_n\) does not converge almost surely. If \(X,X_1,X_2,\ldots\) are independent Bernoulli random variables with parameter \(1/2\), then \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\), while \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>1/2)=1/2\), so convergence in probability fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution; independent Bernoulli constructions show both reverse implications fail.
assumptions_latex: All variables in each implication share a metric state space.
The event sequence in the first counterexample is independent.
The Bernoulli variables in the second counterexample are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implications \(\mathrm{a.s.}\Rightarrow\mathbb{P}\Rightarrow d\) hold, but both converses fail without additional assumptions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical strict implication chain and independent-event counterexamples
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication chain and both counterexamples are standard, and failure_boundary is the correct content kind. A source is absent, and the assumptions should explicitly require a common probability space wherever convergence almost surely or in probability is asserted.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of stochastic-oracle calls needed to attain a declared accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a stochastic oracle \(\mathcal{O}\) that, for a query \(x\), returns random information such as \(g(x,\xi)\). For an algorithm producing \(X_N\) after at most \(N\) oracle calls and an error criterion \(M\), its expected stochastic oracle complexity is \[N_{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon)=\inf\{N\in\mathbb{N}:\mathbb{E}[M(X_N)]\leq\varepsilon\}.\] Its high-probability oracle complexity is \[N_{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf\{N\in\mathbb{N}:\mathbb{P}(M(X_N)\leq\varepsilon)\geq1-\delta\}.\] Batched calls are counted individually unless the oracle model explicitly assigns unit cost to a batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic oracle complexity counts the oracle responses required to meet a stated expected or high-probability error target under an explicit call-cost convention.
assumptions_latex: The oracle interface and the cost of one call are specified.
\(M\) is a declared nonnegative measurable error criterion.
The guarantee mode is either expected or high probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complexity is the least oracle-call budget meeting the declared \(\varepsilon\) or \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) criterion.

notation.meaning: Oracle-call complexity under the stated guarantee mode.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of data samples required to attain a stochastic optimization accuracy target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots\) denote observations drawn or accessed by a stochastic optimization algorithm, and let \(S_T\) be the total number of sample occurrences consumed through budget \(T\), counting repeated uses unless distinct-sample complexity is explicitly requested. For a random output \(X_T\) and error criterion \(M\), expected sample complexity is \[S(\varepsilon)=\inf\{S_T:\mathbb{E}[M(X_T)]\leq\varepsilon\}.\] Under confidence level \(1-\delta\), it is the least \(S_T\) such that \(\mathbb{P}(M(X_T)\leq\varepsilon)\geq1-\delta\). The sampling model must state whether observations are independent, streaming, or drawn from a finite dataset.

\(M\) is a declared nonnegative measurable error criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle–Sample Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion between iteration, oracle-call, and sample-use counts under batching and reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose iteration \(k\) makes \(q_k\) stochastic-oracle calls, call \(j\) consumes \(b_{k,j}\) sample occurrences, and \(D_{k,j}\) is the set of distinct sample identities used by that call. After \(T\) iterations, the exact accounting identities are \[N_{\mathrm{oracle}}(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}q_k,\qquad N_{\mathrm{sample}}(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\sum_{j=1}^{q_k}b_{k,j},\] and \[N_{\mathrm{distinct}}(T)=\left|\bigcup_{k=0}^{T-1}\bigcup_{j=1}^{q_k}D_{k,j}\right|.\] Hence oracle and sample complexities coincide only when every call consumes exactly one sample occurrence; distinct-sample complexity can be smaller under reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle calls, consumed sample occurrences, and distinct samples obey separate counts; they coincide only under one-new-sample-per-call accounting.
assumptions_latex: Each iteration has a finite number \(q_k\) of oracle calls.
Every call has a declared batch size and set of sample identities.
Repeated sample occurrences are counted in \(N_{\mathrm{sample}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{oracle}}=N_{\mathrm{sample}}\) when \(b_{k,j}=1\) for every call, while \(N_{\mathrm{distinct}}\leq N_{\mathrm{sample}}\).

notation.meaning: Number of oracle calls at iteration k.
Number of sample occurrences consumed by a call.
Set of distinct sample identities used by a call.

children.title: Iteration Complexity
children.top_down_role: Accuracy cost measured by stochastic update events.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of algorithmic state updates required for a declared stochastic accuracy guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a stochastic method generate states \(x_0,x_1,\ldots\), with one iteration defined as one complete transition from \(x_k\) to \(x_{k+1}\), regardless of the number of oracle calls or samples used in that transition. For output \(X_T\) and error criterion \(M\), expected iteration complexity is \[T(\varepsilon)=\inf\{T\in\mathbb{N}:\mathbb{E}[M(X_T)]\leq\varepsilon\}.\] High-probability iteration complexity is the least \(T\) such that \(\mathbb{P}(M(X_T)\leq\varepsilon)\geq1-\delta\). Comparisons are meaningful only when the state-transition and output-selection conventions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration complexity counts complete algorithmic updates needed for an expected or high-probability accuracy target, independently of per-iteration data and oracle cost.
assumptions_latex: One iteration is defined by a complete state transition.
\(M\) is a declared nonnegative measurable error criterion.
The output-selection and guarantee modes are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Iteration complexity is the least number of state transitions meeting the declared accuracy criterion.

notation.meaning: Declared algorithm output after T state transitions.

children.title: Epoch Complexity
children.top_down_role: Accuracy cost measured by dataset-equivalent processing cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Epoch Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum SGD complexity measured in completed full-data epochs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), and suppose that each completed epoch processes every index exactly once. If \(K_\varepsilon\) is the least number of completed epochs after which the reported output \(\widehat x\) satisfies an accuracy criterion \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\), then \(K_\varepsilon\) is the epoch complexity. The component-gradient count at that epoch boundary is \(nK_\varepsilon\), apart from separately counted initialization or validation work. If an oracle-call guarantee holds after every call count at least \(N_\varepsilon\), then stopping at the next completed epoch gives the upper bound \(K_\varepsilon\le \lceil N_\varepsilon/n\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epoch complexity counts completed traversals of all n components. An N-call guarantee converts to at most ceiling(N/n) epochs only when it remains valid at the next epoch boundary.
assumptions_latex: Each completed epoch evaluates every component exactly once.
\(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\) specifies the required output accuracy.
For the ceiling conversion, the guarantee holds at every call count at least \(N_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundary evaluation count is \(nK_\varepsilon\), and \(K_\varepsilon\le\lceil N_\varepsilon/n\rceil\) under the stated persistent-guarantee condition.

notation.meaning: component-gradient call threshold for the persistent accuracy guarantee
completed epochs required for accuracy epsilon

children.title: Pass Complexity
children.top_down_role: Accuracy cost measured by complete or effective traversals of finite data.

knowledge_statements.title: Pass Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum oracle cost normalized by dataset size, including partial traversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), let \(N_\varepsilon\) be the total number of component-oracle calls made before the reported output satisfies \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\). The pass complexity is \(P_\varepsilon=N_\varepsilon/n\). This normalization permits fractional passes and applies whether indices are visited cyclically, by reshuffling, or by sampling with replacement, provided repeated calls are counted with multiplicity. If \(T_\varepsilon\) is the number of iterations performed and iteration \(t\) uses a mini-batch of size \(b_t\), then \(N_\varepsilon=\sum_{t=0}^{T_\varepsilon-1}b_t\) and \(P_\varepsilon=n^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T_\varepsilon-1}b_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pass complexity is total component-oracle calls divided by dataset size, with repeated samples counted and partial passes allowed.
assumptions_latex: Every sampled component in a mini-batch incurs one component-oracle call.
\(T_\varepsilon\) is the number of iterations performed before the reported output satisfies \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_\varepsilon=N_\varepsilon/n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T_\varepsilon-1}b_t\).

notation.meaning: number of iterations performed before the accuracy criterion is met

children.title: Streaming-to-Finite-Data Translation
children.top_down_role: Conversion of resource counts between streaming and finite-data regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Streaming-to-Finite-Data Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of streaming oracle counts to empirical finite-sum pass counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\). Conditional on the fixed dataset, draw \(I_t\) independently and uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(g_t=\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)\). Then \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid x_t,F_n]=\nabla F_n(x_t)\), so a streaming analysis requiring \(T_\varepsilon\) independent unbiased oracle calls applies conditionally to this with-replacement empirical oracle whenever its remaining moment assumptions hold. Its finite-data cost is \(T_\varepsilon\) component-gradient evaluations, equivalently \(T_\varepsilon/n\) passes. This translation does not by itself justify random-reshuffling or without-replacement guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform with-replacement sampling turns an empirical finite sum into an unbiased streaming oracle; T calls equal T/n passes, but reshuffling requires separate analysis.
assumptions_latex: Indices are conditionally independent and uniform with replacement.
The streaming theorem's conditional moment assumptions hold for the empirical oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid x_t,F_n]=\nabla F_n(x_t)\) and the normalized data cost is \(T_\varepsilon/n\) passes.

notation.meaning: streaming oracle calls required for accuracy epsilon

children.title: Parallel Execution Complexity Taxonomy

children.title: Parallel Runtime Complexity
children.top_down_role: Wall-clock scaling across workers and computational resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Runtime Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path wall-clock complexity for parallel stochastic first-order execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an accuracy event \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\). For an execution DAG that produces an output satisfying this event, let \(W_\varepsilon\) be its total unit-time work and \(D_\varepsilon\) its critical-path length. On \(P\) identical processors under a greedy scheduler, the parallel runtime obeys \(T_P(\varepsilon)\le W_\varepsilon/P+D_\varepsilon\), up to a scheduler-independent constant and separately charged communication costs. Every schedule also satisfies \(T_P(\varepsilon)\ge\max\{W_\varepsilon/P,D_\varepsilon\}\). Consequently, the achievable speedup is limited by both available parallelism \(W_\varepsilon/D_\varepsilon\) and any communication or synchronization added to the critical path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel time is controlled by work per processor and critical-path depth; speedup stops when depth, communication, or synchronization dominates.
assumptions_latex: The computation is represented by a finite precedence DAG.
Processors are identical and execute ready unit-cost tasks greedily.
Communication not encoded in the DAG is accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{W_\varepsilon/P,D_\varepsilon\}\le T_P(\varepsilon)\lesssim W_\varepsilon/P+D_\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: total work needed to attain accuracy epsilon

children.title: Synchronization Complexity
children.top_down_role: Barrier, communication-round, and coordination costs during parallel execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number and latency cost of global coordination events before certified accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parallel stochastic first-order method, define a synchronization event as a barrier or collective operation that no participating worker can pass until its required messages arrive. If \(S_\varepsilon\) such events occur before the output satisfies \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\), then \(S_\varepsilon\) is the synchronization complexity. If these events are sequentially ordered on a common critical path and event \(s\) has latency \(\lambda_s\), their critical-path contribution is \(C_{\mathrm{sync}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{s=1}^{S_\varepsilon}\lambda_s\). If \(\lambda_s\ge\lambda>0\) for every counted event, then every such execution satisfies \(T_P(\varepsilon)\ge\lambda S_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization complexity counts blocking coordination events. When the events are sequential on one critical path, their latencies add and impose a runtime floor.
assumptions_latex: Each counted synchronization event blocks participating workers until its required messages arrive.
The counted events are sequentially ordered on a common critical path.
Event latency \(\lambda_s\) includes required communication and waiting.
\(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\) defines attainment of the target accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{sync}}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{s=1}^{S_\varepsilon}\lambda_s\), and \(T_P(\varepsilon)\ge\lambda S_\varepsilon\) if \(\lambda_s\ge\lambda>0\).

notation.meaning: number of synchronization events before target accuracy
critical-path latency of synchronization event s
total latency of the sequential synchronization events

children.title: Staleness-Induced Runtime Costs
children.top_down_role: Runtime penalties associated with delayed worker information.

knowledge_statements.title: Staleness-Induced Runtime Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime overhead caused by delayed gradients and their iteration inflation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In asynchronous SGD, write the update as \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t g(x_{t-d_t};\xi_t)\), where \(0\le d_t\le\tau\). Let \(N_\varepsilon(\tau)\) be the number of committed updates required to satisfy \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\), and let \(c_t(\tau)\) be the wall-clock cost of update \(t\), including contention and retries. The staleness-induced runtime cost relative to fresh execution is
\[C_{\mathrm{stale}}(\varepsilon,\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{N_\varepsilon(\tau)-1}c_t(\tau)-\sum_{t=0}^{N_\varepsilon(0)-1}c_t(0).\]
It includes both iteration inflation and per-update systems overhead; bounded delay alone does not imply that this difference is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Staleness cost is the runtime difference between delayed and fresh executions, combining extra optimization updates with contention, retries, and changed per-update cost.
assumptions_latex: Asynchronous updates use gradients delayed by \(d_t\le\tau\).
Fresh and delayed executions use the same target event \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\).
All committed-update costs are measured on a common wall-clock model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{stale}}(\varepsilon,\tau)\) decomposes into update-count inflation and changed per-update execution costs.

notation.meaning: gradient delay at committed update t
updates required under maximum delay tau
runtime difference relative to fresh execution

children.title: Parallel Scaling Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Worker-count regimes limited by serial work, communication, or load imbalance.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Scaling Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work-depth, communication, and serial-fraction limits on SGD speedup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an accuracy-producing execution has total unit-time work \(W_\varepsilon\), one-processor reference time \(T_1(\varepsilon)=W_\varepsilon\), dependency depth \(D_\varepsilon\), unavoidable communication time \(C_\varepsilon(P)\), and unavoidable nonoverlappable serial time \(sT_1(\varepsilon)\) for some \(s\in[0,1]\). Then any \(P\)-processor implementation satisfies \[T_P(\varepsilon)\ge\max\{W_\varepsilon/P,D_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon(P),sT_1(\varepsilon)\}.\] Hence the speedup \(S_P=T_1(\varepsilon)/T_P(\varepsilon)\) satisfies \[S_P\le\min\{P,T_1(\varepsilon)/D_\varepsilon,T_1(\varepsilon)/C_\varepsilon(P),1/s\},\] with the last term omitted when \(s=0\). Strong scaling saturates when dependency depth, communication, or serial work dominates \(W_\varepsilon/P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a unit-work serial baseline, parallel speedup is limited by processor count, dependency depth, communication, and the reciprocal nonoverlappable serial fraction.
assumptions_latex: All compared executions satisfy the same accuracy event.
The one-processor reference time satisfies \(T_1(\varepsilon)=W_\varepsilon\) in the unit-cost work model.
\(D_\varepsilon\), \(C_\varepsilon(P)\), and \(sT_1(\varepsilon)\) are individually unavoidable runtime lower bounds.
The serial time \(sT_1(\varepsilon)\) cannot overlap parallel work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_P\le\min\{P,T_1(\varepsilon)/D_\varepsilon,T_1(\varepsilon)/C_\varepsilon(P),1/s\}\) for \(s>0\).

notation.meaning: speedup relative to the one-processor reference execution
total unit-time work required for the accuracy event
fraction of one-processor time that is unavoidable and nonoverlappable

children.title: Stochastic First-Order Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Information-theoretic boundaries for stochastic convex and nonconvex optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic First-Order Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical oracle lower-bound regimes for convex and smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the stochastic first-order oracle model, worst-case query complexity depends on the function class. For convex \(G\)-Lipschitz objectives over a domain with initial distance at most \(R\), attaining \(\mathbb E[F(\widehat x)-F^*]\le\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\) oracle calls in general. For \(\mu\)-strongly convex objectives with gradient-noise variance at most \(\sigma^2\), the stochastic term is \(\Omega(\sigma^2/(\mu\varepsilon))\). For smooth nonconvex objectives with smoothness \(L\), initial gap \(\Delta\), and variance \(\sigma^2\), obtaining \(\mathbb E\|\nabla F(\widehat x)\|\le\varepsilon\) has a canonical stochastic lower-bound scale \(\Omega(\sigma^2L\Delta/\varepsilon^4)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case stochastic first-order complexity scales quadratically in convex accuracy, linearly in inverse strongly convex accuracy, and quartically for nonconvex gradient-norm accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns unbiased stochastic first-order information with the stated variance control.
The algorithm is measured by worst-case expected oracle queries over the specified class.
The convex and nonconvex regimes are interpreted separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The respective lower-bound scales are \(\Omega(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\), \(\Omega(\sigma^2/(\mu\varepsilon))\), and \(\Omega(\sigma^2L\Delta/\varepsilon^4)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No sources are supplied for three nontrivial lower bounds. Authoritative results are required to fix the oracle model, randomized-algorithm scope, dimension or parameter regimes, and the nonconvex norm-versus-squared-norm accuracy convention.

children.title: Objective-Value Certificates
children.top_down_role: Observable or estimable evidence based on objective accuracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Value Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability bounds certifying the objective value of an SGD output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x;\xi)]\), and let \(\widehat x\) be independent of a validation sample \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\). An objective-value certificate at confidence \(1-\delta\) is a random interval \([L_m,U_m]\), computable from the validation data and declared concentration assumptions, such that
\[\mathbb P\{L_m\le F(\widehat x)\le U_m\}\ge1-\delta.\]
Its width \(U_m-L_m\) quantifies certified evaluation uncertainty. It certifies objective accuracy relative to a target value \(v\) when the relevant one-sided bound holds, for example \(U_m\le v+\varepsilon\). Independence may be replaced only by a concentration argument valid for adaptive reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validation-based confidence interval certifies the population objective at the SGD output; comparison of its upper endpoint with a target yields an accuracy certificate.
assumptions_latex: The validation observations satisfy a stated concentration condition.
The output is independent of validation data, unless adaptive concentration is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{L_m\le F(\widehat x)\le U_m\}\ge1-\delta\).

children.title: Optimality-Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Accuracy evidence based on primal, dual, or primal-dual gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality-Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual or lower-bound certificates for convex stochastic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a proper closed convex objective with optimum \(F^*\). Suppose a computable random upper bound \(U\) and lower bound \(L\) satisfy \(\mathbb P\{F(\widehat x)\le U\text{ and }L\le F^*\}\ge1-\delta\). Then \(G=U-L\) is an optimality-gap certificate: whenever \(G\le\varepsilon\),
\[\mathbb P\{F(\widehat x)-F^*\le\varepsilon\}\ge1-\delta.
\]
In a primal-dual formulation, \(U=F(\widehat x)\) and \(L=D(\widehat y)\) are admissible when \(\widehat x\) and \(\widehat y\) are feasible and weak duality gives \(D(\widehat y)\le F^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid objective upper bound minus a valid optimum lower bound certifies suboptimality; a feasible primal-dual gap is the standard instance.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, convex, and attains its optimum.
The upper and lower bounds are jointly valid with probability at least \(1-\delta\).
Any primal-dual specialization satisfies primal and dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=U-L\le\varepsilon\) certifies \(F(\widehat x)-F^*\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: certified upper bound on the candidate objective
certified lower bound on the optimal value

children.title: Distance-to-Solution Certificates
children.top_down_role: Accuracy evidence based on distance to a solution set or reference point.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-to-Solution Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability certification of distance from an SGD output to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be proper, closed, and convex on a closed convex set \(X\), with nonempty solution set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x)\). A radius \(r\ge0\), computed from declared stochastic observations and assumptions, is a \((1-\delta)\)-confidence distance certificate for \(\widehat x\in X\) if
\[\mathbb P\{\operatorname{dist}(\widehat x,X^*)\le r\}\ge1-\delta.
\]
For example, if \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and a valid gap certificate gives \(F(\widehat x)-F^*\le\varepsilon\), then \(r=\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\mu}\) is a distance certificate on the same event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distance certificate bounds the output's distance to the solution set with stated confidence; strong convexity converts an objective-gap certificate into such a radius.
assumptions_latex: The convex solution set \(X^*\) is nonempty.
The claimed radius is measurable from the certificate data.
For the conversion example, \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{\operatorname{dist}(\widehat x,X^*)\le r\}\ge1-\delta\), with \(r=\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\mu}\) under strong convexity and an \(\varepsilon\)-gap certificate.

children.title: Certificate Conversion Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometry-dependent translation among value, gap, and distance measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Conversion Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversions among objective-gap, distance, and residual certificates under convex regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be convex with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\), and write \(\Delta(x)=F(x)-F^*\). Certificate conversions require additional geometry. If \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\sqrt{2\Delta(x)/\mu}\). If \(F\) is \(G\)-Lipschitz on its domain, then \(\Delta(x)\le G\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\). If \(F\) is differentiable and \(L\)-smooth, then \(\|\nabla F(x)\|^2\le2L\Delta(x)\). Each deterministic implication preserves the confidence level of the source stochastic certificate; reversing any implication generally requires a corresponding error-bound, growth, or strong-convexity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity, Lipschitz continuity, and smoothness convert gap, distance, and gradient certificates; confidence is preserved, while reverse conversions need extra error-bound geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is convex and attains its minimum.
Each displayed conversion uses its stated regularity condition.
The source certificate is valid on an event of probability at least \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On the source event, \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\sqrt{2\Delta(x)/\mu}\), \(\Delta(x)\le G\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\), or \(\|\nabla F(x)\|^2\le2L\Delta(x)\), as applicable.

children.title: First-Order Residual Certificate Family

children.title: Gradient-Norm Certificates
children.top_down_role: First-order stopping evidence based on smooth gradient magnitude.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Norm Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability first-order certificate for smooth unconstrained stochastic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, let \(X\) be a possibly random candidate iterate, and let \(U\) be a data-dependent statistic satisfying \(\mathbb{P}(\|\nabla F(X)\|\le U)\ge 1-\alpha\). Declaring success when \(U\le\varepsilon\) is a level-\(1-\alpha\) gradient-norm certificate: \[\mathbb{P}\bigl(U\le\varepsilon\ \text{and}\ \|\nabla F(X)\|>\varepsilon\bigr)\le\alpha.\] Thus an accepted certificate verifies \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity except on an event of probability at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid upper confidence bound on the gradient norm certifies approximate stationarity whenever that bound is at most the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) upper-bounds \(\|\nabla F(X)\|\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(U\le\varepsilon,\ \|\nabla F(X)\|>\varepsilon)\le\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Statistical upper bound on the gradient norm.

children.title: Gradient-Mapping Certificates
children.top_down_role: First-order stopping evidence adapted to constraints or composite structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|G_\eta(x)\|\le\varepsilon\), with \(G_\eta(x)=0\iff 0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\).

notation.meaning: Proximal operator of eta times h.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite first-order certificate based on the proximal-gradient mapping.

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=f+h\), \(\eta>0\), and \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), define the gradient mapping by \[G_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\bigr).\] A verified inequality \(\|G_\eta(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-gradient-mapping certificate. Moreover, \(G_\eta(x)=0\) holds if and only if \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\); hence the zero certificate is equivalent to first-order stationarity for the composite problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal-gradient mapping measures composite stationarity; a mapping norm at most the nonnegative tolerance certifies an approximate fixed point, and a zero norm exactly characterizes stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Mapping Certificates

children.title: Proximal-Residual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Stopping evidence based on proximal fixed-point residuals.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,A(J_{\eta A}x))\le r_\eta(x)\), and \(r_\eta(x)=0\iff 0\in A(x)\).

notation.meaning: Distance from zero to the set A(y).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent fixed-point certificate for a monotone inclusion.

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^d\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^d\) be maximally monotone, let \(\eta>0\), let \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and let \(J_{\eta A}=(I+\eta A)^{-1}\). Define \[r_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}\|x-J_{\eta A}(x)\|.\] The inequality \(r_\eta(x)\le\varepsilon\) is a proximal-residual certificate. If \(y=J_{\eta A}(x)\), then \(\eta^{-1}(x-y)\in A(y)\), so \(\operatorname{dist}(0,A(y))\le r_\eta(x)\). In particular, \(r_\eta(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in A(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled displacement from a point to its resolvent image certifies a nearby inclusion residual at a specified nonnegative tolerance and vanishes exactly at a solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Residual Certificates

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Residual Comparison Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem classes where first-order residual measures are comparable or distinct.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Comparison Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of composite stationarity residuals under Lipschitz smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+h\), let \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\), and let \(G_\eta(x)=(x-y)/\eta\). If \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(y))\le(1+L\eta)\|G_\eta(x)\|.\] If additionally \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial h\), then \[\|G_\eta(x)\|\le\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x)).\] Consequently, gradient-mapping and subdifferential residuals are comparable, although generally evaluated at different points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth-plus-convex objectives, the gradient-mapping norm bounds a stationarity residual at the proximal point and is itself bounded by the residual at the original point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(y))\le(1+L\eta)\|G_\eta(x)\|\), and when \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial h\), \(\|G_\eta(x)\|\le\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\).

notation.meaning: Composite limiting subdifferential, equal here to gradient f plus convex subdifferential h.

children.title: Statistical Stopping Rules
children.top_down_role: Termination criteria based on estimated uncertainty from noisy observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Stopping Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-inspection stopping using a confidence bound on a stationarity measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix deterministic inspection times \(1\le t_1<\cdots<t_K\), error allocations \(\alpha_k>0\) with \(\sum_{k=1}^K\alpha_k\le\alpha\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At inspection \(t_k\), construct an upper confidence bound \(U_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb{P}(R(x_{t_k})>U_k)\le\alpha_k\). Stop at the first \(t_k\) for which \(U_k\le\varepsilon\), and output \(x_{t_k}\); otherwise return no certificate. The probability of stopping with \(R(x_{t_k})>\varepsilon\) is at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inspect predetermined iterates, stop when a multiplicity-adjusted upper confidence bound falls below tolerance, and control the probability of a false stationarity declaration.
assumptions_latex: \(t_1,\ldots,t_K\) are fixed before observing the inspection data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(\text{stop and output }x\text{ with }R(x)>\varepsilon)\le\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Upper confidence bound at inspection k.
Error probability assigned to inspection k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Bonferroni-calibrated fixed-inspection confidence bounds control false stopping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Bonferroni-calibrated fixed-inspection algorithm is correct and fits Statistical Stopping Rules, but it has no authoritative citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Sequential Stopping Rules
children.top_down_role: Termination criteria based on evidence accumulated during repeated monitoring.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Stopping Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive stopping based on an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\ge1}\) be a filtration, let \(x_t\) be \(\mathcal{F}_t\)-measurable, and suppose \((U_t)_{t\ge1}\) satisfies \[\mathbb{P}\bigl(\forall t\ge1:\ R(x_t)\le U_t\bigr)\ge1-\alpha.\] Define the stopping time \(\tau=\inf\{t\ge1:U_t\le\varepsilon\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=\infty\). If \(\tau<\infty\), output \(x_\tau\); otherwise continue sampling. Then \(\mathbb{P}(\tau<\infty,\ R(x_\tau)>\varepsilon)\le\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An anytime-valid upper confidence sequence permits adaptive stopping while retaining the prescribed probability of a correct stationarity certificate.
assumptions_latex: \((U_t)\) simultaneously upper-bounds \(R(x_t)\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(\tau<\infty,\ R(x_\tau)>\varepsilon)\le\alpha\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simultaneous coverage remains valid at data-dependent stopping times

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The anytime-valid stopping rule and its false-certificate guarantee are correct and algorithm is the appropriate content kind, but no authoritative confidence-sequence or sequential-inference source is cited.

children.title: Confidence Calibration
children.top_down_role: Calibration of stopping evidence to target reliability levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error-budget calibration for repeated stochastic stationarity checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For inspection events \(E_t=\{R(x_t)>U_t\}\), choose deterministic error levels \(\alpha_t>0\) satisfying \(\sum_{t\ge1}\alpha_t\le\alpha\). If each marginal construction obeys \(\mathbb{P}(E_t)\le\alpha_t\), then \[\mathbb{P}\bigl(\exists t\ge1:R(x_t)>U_t\bigr)\le\sum_{t\ge1}\alpha_t\le\alpha.\] Therefore the bounds are jointly valid at confidence \(1-\alpha\), and any stopping rule that accepts only when \(U_t\le\varepsilon\) has false-certificate probability at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate a summable error budget across inspections; the resulting bounds are simultaneously valid and can safely support adaptive stopping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(\exists t\ge1:R(x_t)>U_t)\le\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Confidence-bound failure event at time t.
Error budget assigned to time t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: countable union bound provides simultaneous confidence calibration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The summable error-budget calibration follows from the countable union bound and fits the Confidence Calibration leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative source or locator.

children.title: Optional-Stopping Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Validity limits caused by adaptive inspection or data-dependent termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Optional-Stopping Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ville-type time-uniform boundary for a sub-gamma process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((S_t,\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\ge0}\) be adapted and let \((V_t)_{t\ge0}\) be predictable and nonnegative. Suppose that for a fixed \(\lambda>0\), \(M_t=\exp\{\lambda S_t-\psi(\lambda)V_t\}\) is a nonnegative supermartingale with \(M_0\le1\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define \[b_t(\alpha,\lambda)=\frac{\log(1/\alpha)+\psi(\lambda)V_t}{\lambda}.\] Then \(\mathbb{P}(\exists t\ge0:S_t\ge b_t(\alpha,\lambda))\le\alpha\). Consequently the same boundary remains valid when evaluated at any stopping time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative exponential supermartingale yields a time-uniform crossing boundary whose error probability remains controlled under optional stopping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(\exists t\ge0:S_t\ge b_t(\alpha,\lambda))\le\alpha\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Ville inequality applied to a nonnegative exponential supermartingale

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated boundary is a correct Ville-inequality consequence of the assumed nonnegative supermartingale, and theorem is the correct terminal role. An authoritative source with a theorem, section, or page locator is nevertheless required.

children.title: Uniform Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Full-history averaging with equal contribution from retained iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-history arithmetic averaging of stochastic-approximation iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\), initialize \(\bar x_1=x_1\) and update \[\bar x_t=\bar x_{t-1}+\frac{1}{t}(x_t-\bar x_{t-1}),\qquad t=2,\ldots,T.\] Output \(\bar x_T\). Equivalently, \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\). Every iterate receives weight \(1/T\), so the procedure is the uniform full-history averaging policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain the arithmetic mean of all iterates using an online recursion and return that mean after the final iteration.

children.title: Weighted Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Full-history averaging with nonuniform iterate contributions.

notation.meaning: Weighted average through time t whenever the cumulative weight is positive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-history averaging with deterministic nonnegative iterate weights.

source_refs.locator: 8.3 The Stochastic Projected Subgradient Method p. 221
source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(T\ge1\), iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and deterministic weights \(w_t\ge0\) with \(W_T=\sum_{t=1}^T w_t>0\), define \[\bar x_T^{(w)}=\frac{1}{W_T}\sum_{t=1}^T w_t x_t.\] For an online implementation, set \(W_0=0\), update \(W_t=W_{t-1}+w_t\), let \(t_0=\min\{t:w_t>0\}\), initialize \(\bar x_{t_0}^{(w)}=x_{t_0}\), and for \(t>t_0\) update \[\bar x_t^{(w)}=\bar x_{t-1}^{(w)}+\frac{w_t}{W_t}\bigl(x_t-\bar x_{t-1}^{(w)}\bigr).\] Output \(\bar x_T^{(w)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Form a convex combination of the full iterate history using prescribed nonnegative weights, initializing the running mean at the first positively weighted iterate and then applying the weighted-mean recursion.

children.title: Weight-Schedule Regimes
children.top_down_role: Polynomial, recency-sensitive, or gain-linked weighting families.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Schedule Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity regimes for normalized full-history averaging weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative weights \((w_t)_{t\ge1}\), write \(W_T=\sum_{t=1}^T w_t\) and \(q_{T,t}=w_t/W_T\). A diffuse full-history schedule satisfies \[W_T\to\infty,\qquad \max_{1\le t\le T}q_{T,t}\to0.\] Its variance concentration is measured by \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)=(\sum_{t=1}^T q_{T,t}^2)^{-1}=W_T^2/\sum_{t=1}^T w_t^2\). For polynomial weights \(w_t=t^p\) with \(p>-1/2\), \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)/T\to(2p+1)/(p+1)^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular averaging schedule has diverging total weight and no dominant iterate; its squared normalized weights determine an effective sample size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{t\le T}q_{T,t}\to0\), with \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)=W_T^2/\sum_{t=1}^T w_t^2\) and polynomial-weight limit \((2p+1)/(p+1)^2\).

notation.meaning: Weight of iterate t after normalization at horizon T.
Effective sample size induced by normalized weights.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: normalized-weight diffuseness and inverse squared-weight concentration characterize averaging schedules

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diffuseness conditions, effective-sample-size expression, and polynomial-weight limit are mathematically coherent and condition is a reasonable role for the schedule-regime leaf. The quantitative asymptotic claim requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Tail-Averaging Transient Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Averaging restricted to later iterates to reduce transient effects.

children.title: Tail Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaging policies restricted to a terminal segment of the iterate history.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform averaging after discarding an initial stochastic-approximation transient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and a burn-in index \(b\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}\), define the tail length \(m=T-b\) and output \[\bar x_{b:T}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{t=b+1}^{T}x_t.\] Online computation initializes \(z_{b+1}=x_{b+1}\) and updates \(z_t=z_{t-1}+(x_t-z_{t-1})/(t-b)\) for \(t>b+1\). The discarded prefix contributes zero weight and each retained iterate receives weight \(1/m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard the first b iterates, uniformly average the remaining tail, and return the resulting mean to reduce initialization transients.

notation.meaning: Uniform average over the retained tail.

children.title: Burn-In Selection
children.top_down_role: Choice of the transient period excluded before averaging begins.

knowledge_statements.title: Burn-In Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for selecting the discarded prefix in tail-averaged stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given iterates \(x_0,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d\), choose a burn-in index \(b\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and form \(\bar x_{b:n}=(n-b)^{-1}\sum_{k=b+1}^{n}x_k\). For a target \(x_\star\), an oracle mean-square-error burn-in is any \[b_n^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le b<n}\left\{\left\|\mathbb E[\bar x_{b:n}]-x_\star\right\|^2+\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\operatorname{Cov}(\bar x_{b:n})\right)\right\}.\] Thus burn-in selection balances removal of initialization bias against the variance increase caused by reducing the retained sample size \(n-b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select the discarded prefix by minimizing the tail average’s squared bias plus covariance trace; longer burn-in reduces initialization effects but leaves fewer iterates for variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_n^\star\) minimizes the mean-square error of \(\bar x_{b:n}\) over admissible burn-in indices.

notation.meaning: average of iterates retained after burn-in

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bias-variance decomposition of the mean-square error gives the stated oracle selection criterion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle MSE criterion is mathematically coherent, all notation is introduced, and condition is a suitable content kind for this terminal container. However, the record has no inspectable citation or source locator supporting its use as a burn-in selection criterion for tail-averaged stochastic approximation.

children.title: Transient–Variance Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Finite-time balance between transient removal and retained-sample variability.

knowledge_statements.title: Transient–Variance Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bias–variance tradeoff induced by changing the retained tail of an iterate sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every burn-in \(b<n\), the tail average satisfies \[\mathbb E\|\bar x_{b:n}-x_\star\|^2=\|\mathbb E\bar x_{b:n}-x_\star\|^2+\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\operatorname{Cov}(\bar x_{b:n})\right).\] Increasing \(b\) can suppress the transient component \(\|\mathbb E\bar x_{b:n}-x_\star\|^2\), but it does not universally improve total error: under weak dependence in a stationary tail with long-run covariance \(V\), the variance term is asymptotically \(\operatorname{tr}(V)/(n-b)\). Consequently, discarding more iterates trades smaller transient bias for a shorter effective sample and potentially larger variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail averaging decomposes into transient bias and sampling variance. Discarding more early iterates can reduce bias, but the shorter retained tail typically increases variance.
assumptions_latex: For the asymptotic variance assertion, the retained stationary tail obeys a central limit theorem with long-run covariance \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tail length and transient suppression must be balanced because the two mean-square-error components generally move in opposite directions.

notation.meaning: long-run covariance of the stationary or locally stationary tail

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact bias-variance identity plus the standard long-run-covariance scaling for sample means
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact bias-variance identity fits the property container. The long-run covariance approximation additionally requires a clearly specified joint regime for the retained length n-b and a source stating the relevant dependence and central-limit assumptions. No citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Forgetting-Based Averaging Family
children.top_down_role: Forgetting-based averages for tracking and constant-gain regimes.

children.title: Exponential Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Recency-weighted averaging with exponentially decaying historical influence.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive iterate averaging with geometrically decaying weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input iterates \(x_0,x_1,\ldots\in\mathbb R^d\), forgetting parameters \(\beta_k\in(0,1]\), and initialize \(y_0=x_0\). For \(k\ge1\), update \[y_k=(1-\beta_k)y_{k-1}+\beta_k x_k.\] Equivalently, \(y_k=w_{0,k}x_0+\sum_{i=1}^k w_{i,k}x_i\), where \(w_{0,k}=\prod_{j=1}^k(1-\beta_j)\) and \(w_{i,k}=\beta_i\prod_{j=i+1}^k(1-\beta_j)\). The weights are nonnegative and sum to one. At a prescribed stopping index \(n\), output \(y_n\). For constant \(\beta_k=\beta\), the weight of an observation \(r\) steps old is proportional to \((1-\beta)^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a recursive convex combination of the current iterate and the previous average. Constant forgetting gives geometrically decaying weights to older iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_n\) is a convex, exponentially forgetting average of \(x_0,\ldots,x_n\).

notation.meaning: forgetting or averaging parameter at iteration k
weight assigned at time k to iterate i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unrolling the exponential-smoothing recursion yields the displayed normalized weights
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursion and its unrolled convex weights are correct, and algorithm is the appropriate content kind. Geometric or exponential decay is guaranteed for constant beta, whereas arbitrary varying beta_k produces product-form forgetting that need not be geometric. An inspectable source is also absent.

children.title: Moving-Window Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaging over a finite rolling segment of recent iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Moving-Window Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform averaging over a fixed or time-varying trailing window.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input iterates \(x_0,x_1,\ldots\in\mathbb R^d\) and window lengths \(m_k\in\{1,\ldots,k+1\}\). At iteration \(k\), compute \[y_k=\frac1{m_k}\sum_{i=k-m_k+1}^{k}x_i.\] For a constant window \(m_k=m\) once \(k\ge m-1\), the update can be implemented recursively as \(y_k=y_{k-1}+m^{-1}(x_k-x_{k-m})\). At a prescribed stopping index \(n\), output \(y_n\). Iterates older than \(m_n-1\) steps receive zero weight, while all retained iterates receive weight \(1/m_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average only the most recent window of iterates. A fixed window admits a constant-cost update by adding the newest iterate and removing the oldest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_n\) is the uniform average of the final \(m_n\) iterates.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct definition and algebraic recursion for a trailing arithmetic mean
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The window-average definition fits the algorithm container. For a fixed window m, the recursive update involving x_{k-m} is valid from k at least m, not at the first index k=m-1 where the full window becomes available. No inspectable citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Forgetting-Horizon Regimes
children.top_down_role: Effective memory choices for stationary, drifting, or constant-gain settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Forgetting-Horizon Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of exponential averaging by its effective memory relative to elapsed time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constant forgetting \(\beta\in(0,1]\), define the effective horizon \(h_\beta=1/\beta\); exponential weights beyond age \(r\) have total mass \((1-\beta)^{r+1}\). For a sequence \(\beta_n\downarrow0\), the regimes are: \(n\beta_n\to\infty\), where \(h_{\beta_n}=o(n)\) and averaging is localized to a vanishing fraction of the history; \(n\beta_n\to c\in(0,\infty)\), where the horizon is of order \(n\); and \(n\beta_n\to0\), where the nominal horizon exceeds the observed history and forgetting is negligible over \(n\) steps. A moving window has the analogous classification after replacing \(h_{\beta_n}\) by \(m_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective memory is about the inverse forgetting rate. It may cover a vanishing, fixed-order, or effectively complete fraction of the observed history.
assumptions_latex: For the window analogue, \(1\le m_n\le n+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limits of \(n\beta_n\), equivalently of \(h_{\beta_n}/n\), determine the finite-, macroscopic-, and full-history regimes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: geometric-tail mass and comparison of the inverse forgetting rate with elapsed time give the regime classification
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inverse-forgetting-horizon comparisons are algebraically consistent and property fits the terminal container. The labels and the claimed moving-window analogy require a source with a specific locator, especially because the exponential scheme is truncated by the observed history. No citation is provided.

children.title: Asymptotic Normality of Averaged Approximation
children.top_down_role: Central-limit theory for averaged stochastic approximation near stable solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Normality of Averaged Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyak–Ruppert central limit theorem for a locally stable finite-dimensional stochastic approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\gamma_{k+1}(h(x_k)+\xi_{k+1})\) converge in probability to \(x_\star\), where \(h(x_\star)=0\), \(h(x)=H(x-x_\star)+o(\|x-x_\star\|)\), and every eigenvalue of \(H\) has positive real part. Suppose \(\xi_{k+1}\) is a martingale difference, its conditional covariance converges in probability to \(\Gamma\), a local Lindeberg condition holds, and \(\gamma_k=a k^{-\alpha}\) with \(a>0\) and \(1/2<\alpha<1\). For \(\bar x_n=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n x_k\), \[\sqrt n(\bar x_n-x_\star)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,H^{-1}\Gamma H^{-\mathsf T}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under local stability, martingale-noise, and diminishing-gain conditions, the equally averaged approximation is asymptotically normal with the sandwich covariance.
assumptions_latex: The recursion converges to a locally differentiable stable root with nonsingular Jacobian \(H\).
The martingale noise satisfies conditional covariance convergence and a local Lindeberg condition.

children.title: Asymptotic Efficiency of Averaged Approximation
children.top_down_role: Efficiency comparisons with benchmark recursive-estimation covariance limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Efficiency of Averaged Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gain-robust sandwich covariance and its recursive-estimation efficiency interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the hypotheses of the Polyak–Ruppert central limit theorem, the averaged estimator has limiting covariance \(V_{\mathrm{PR}}=H^{-1}\Gamma H^{-\mathsf T}\), which does not depend on the scalar gain multiplier \(a>0\) when \(1/2<\alpha<1\). Hence averaging attains the standard sandwich covariance for the estimating equation \(h(x_\star)=0\). Whenever the underlying statistical experiment has information bound \(H^{-1}\Gamma H^{-\mathsf T}\), the averaged approximation is asymptotically efficient. In particular, for a correctly specified likelihood score with \(H=\Gamma=I(x_\star)\), its limiting covariance is \(I(x_\star)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyak–Ruppert averaging removes first-order dependence on the gain multiplier and attains the sandwich benchmark; for likelihood scores this becomes inverse Fisher information.
assumptions_latex: The averaged-approximation central limit theorem holds with nonsingular \(H\).
Efficiency is asserted only when the model’s information lower bound equals the displayed sandwich covariance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_{\mathrm{PR}}=H^{-1}\Gamma H^{-\mathsf T}\), and this covariance is efficient whenever it equals the experiment-specific information bound.

notation.meaning: asymptotic covariance of the averaged approximation
Fisher information at the target parameter

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the Polyak-Ruppert sandwich covariance is gain-robust and coincides with inverse Fisher information in the correctly specified score case
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
